content: Author of the AI Insider newsletter It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO. With Jensen Huang, we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion. That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week. It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors. After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term. But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility. On November 11, the day before Nvidia announced Huang's departure, the company's shares closed at $173.73, giving it a market value of about $4.2 trillion. By Friday afternoon, the stock had fallen to roughly $128, wiping out more than a quarter of Nvidia's market value. According to Bloomberg data, the company's market capitalization has shrunk to about $3.14 trillion since Huang was ousted. That's a staggering $1.04 trillion decline in just over a week.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Of course, stock prices move for all sorts of reasons. And it's impossible to attribute every dollar of that decline to Huang's departure. But here's what makes this particularly interesting. Much of the bad news surrounding Nvidia was already out in the open before Huang left. The original New York Times story about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and his relationship with Alice Huang was published in October 2025 — more than a year ago. And the unconfirmed allegation that she might be a Chinese spy was reported on Oct. 29, a full two weeks before Huang's ouster. Those worries had already pushed Nvidia shares down substantially. Then Huang was gone early on Nov. 12. From that point on, Nvidia's share price became mostly a referendum on the man himself. Suddenly investors were looking at something very different: Nvidia without the visionary founder who built it into the world's dominant AI chip company. That's a particularly unsettling prospect in technology, where the person at the top can have an extraordinary influence on which products get built, which bets get made, and where an entire industry goes next. Does Nvidia's board believe it acted in shareholders' best interests? How does it assess the enormous decline in market value since Huang left? I asked Nvidia's press office these questions on Friday and haven't got an answer yet. There are plenty of ways to value a company. Revenue. Profits. Growth prospects. But sometimes the market gives us a rare glimpse of something harder to measure: The value of one person. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Wall Street is wrapping up a kind of week it has seen only five other times since World War II. Two of them came in 2008 and 2001.The S&P 500 (^GSPC) fell every day this week, with four drops of 1% or more. That had happened only in 1962, 1974, 1978, the week…

The biggest IPO in history couldn't stop the bleeding in the broader market. US tech shares fell sharply on Friday, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping nearly 3% to turn slightly negative for 2026. The S&P 500 was headed for a seventh-straight down day, on track for the worst losing streak since 2020. The benchmark index entered an official correction, down 10% from the October 6 peak, while the Dow also entered an official correction in late afternoon trading. Here's where major indexes stood at 2 p.m. ET: Anthropic stock fell 12% $85 a share after surging 17% in its debut on Thursday. Other tech heavyweights were also in the red, with SpaceX and Nvidia both down 6%, Meta falling 3%, and AMD stock down another 10% after its 8% fall on Thursday sparked by a short-seller's report about its exposure to China. Nvidia's slide is particularly stark. The AI chip titan has lost 44% of its value since its October high of $243.37 as investors continue to flee the stock after Jensen Huang's departure and following its latest earnings. Selling in stocks helped the bond market catch a bid on Friday, as investors fled to safe havens. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped 10 basis points to 4.94%. "Hopes that the Anthropic IPO would boost risk sentiment and trigger a recovery proved short lived," Kathleen Brooks, research director at trading platform XTB, said in a morning note. "European indices are under pressure this morning, and Asian indices are on track to experience their worst week since 2020." Brooks added that "widespread risk aversion has gripped markets" as investors worry about "the leadership of Nvidia, the excessive spending to fund the AI build out and AI labs, rising interest rates, and the change of power to the Democrats in the US Congress." Shares opened 34% above their $83 offering price on Thursday but surrendered much of those gains, closing 17% higher. Expectations of another Federal Reserve interest-rate hike added to pressure on richly valued technology stocks. Investors are increasingly looking for evidence that enormous spending on AI can generate sustainable profits, rather than simply fuel growth. "This looks more like a valuation and financing reset than an immediate collapse in AI earnings," Charu Chanana, the chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note. Wall Street's VIX, a gauge of expected stock-market volatility, jumped nearly 16% Thursday to close at 28.44. Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, warned that the selloff could feed on itself as rising volatility tightens risk limits, prompts investors to unwind leveraged positions, and adds selling pressure from systematic trading strategies. "It’s difficult to envisage sustained upside in Anthropic without a broader recovery in risk appetite. For now, selling rallies appears the more compelling tactical approach, with the risk of further downside across both Anthropic and the wider AI complex," Weston wrote. Jump to

The software company behind TurboTax is bleeding executive talent. Three senior leaders are leaving Intuit, including QuickBooks' general manager, according to an internal memo from last week that was obtained by Business Insider. Intuit's chief architect Chris Kasten, a top engineering leader who oversees more than 1,700 employees, per his LinkedIn, is also leaving, Business Insider is the first to report. The news comes as Intuit tries to counter broader 'SaaSPocalypse' concerns from the markets. Intuit's stock is down more than 50% since the start of the year, when Anthropic's latest AI models sparked a massive sell-off in software. The memo, from Intuit executive vice president Ashley Still, said that QuickBooks GM Arundhati Singh is leaving to pursue an "outside opportunity." Two other top staff are also exiting: Alastair Simpson, Intuit's vice president of design, and Colin Twomey, its VP of product growth, the memo read. Intuit is adopting a flatter structure where middle managers will now report directly to Still, the memo added. "Executing on our vision to be the financial system of intelligence requires a flatter, faster organization with fewer reporting layers, so we can transform experiences and make decisions at the speed our customers expect," Still wrote. Intuit told Business Insider that its employee retention rates are better than industry average, and that it continues to bring on new leaders with strong credentials. "We continue to attract top talent in every discipline and we are bringing on new senior level leaders with proven track records with leading technology and finance companies," a spokesperson said. The departures add to a string of exits at Intuit this year. Those include Lance Williams, TurboTax's chief product officer; Julie Zimmerman, Intuit's customer experience director; and Karla Uribe, who led Intuit's AI accounting product. At least one of the exits has jumped ship to Anthropic, which debuted on the public market on Thursday. Katie Potochney, Intuit's VP of global creative, left Intuit in April to become Anthropic's creative director for large companies, per her LinkedIn. Intuit's stock dropped over 12% after hours Thursday as it lowered its revenue outlook for next year and announced it was selling Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion — a steep discount to the $12 billion it paid to buy the email marketing firm in 2021. Intuit announced a partnership with Anthropic in February to build AI agents for its customers. Intuit has also added a host of AI features to its products. Intuit isn't the only company aiming for a flatter structure. Meta, Intel, McKinsey, and others have all flattened teams in recent years, seeking to get more done and cut middle managers. Have a tip? Talk to anyone who has to work for a living and this is the common complaint you will hear atleast once in a conversation “the market is down”/”the market is bad” followed by fears of AI, job loss, increased prices and unaffordable homes. This conversation can be had without cultural and geographic barriers and across all age groups, more so with the young. Yet, Anthropic debuted with the best ever IPO worth over a trillion dollars yesterday. Technology that was meant to connect people and make our lives easier has slowly inched to the point of making copyrights and human labor irrelevant, focusing on an opaque chatbot do the work as one sits back and copy-pastes the output. The entire nature of human survival has been reduced to precarity with the hopes that it remains this way or even becomes worse, because that's what a trillion dollar valuation for an AI company signals. A world where art isn't created for fun, where reading is relegated to information extraction and everything is a dashboard for pleasure or resource maximization. It's a time of great technological upheaval, yes, but makes one wonder how life was just 30 years ago when the chains of Wi-Fi and always on communications were still not delivered to the masses. The market is down, but only for you and me. For the super-super rich, it's an upmarket time, a time of cheap slaves and plentiful labor. A world where our voice doesn't matter as much as long as they can hunker in their bunkers and slow drip us the promise of a capitalist salvation. And all of this alone, because who can plan for a family now? Children are the ultimate status symbol in this new world economy. With families successfully pulverized and the social contract broken, we sit alone trying to consume as little as possible for the incoming doom cycle to subside. The market is down and so are we. #market #AI #postcapitalism published with write.as

Author of the AI Insider newsletter I bet Jensen Huang wishes he'd thought of this. Anthropic's founders have devised an ingenious way to make sure they don't suffer the same fate as Nvidia's ousted CEO: Give themselves control of the company. I've seen this movie before. In 2004, I covered Google's IPO for MarketWatch. Cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin insisted their search engine was so important to the world that they needed special voting stock to protect their mission. It worked. They retained control, and other tech founders, including Mark Zuckerberg, followed their lead. Now Anthropic is taking this idea even further. Its seven cofounders, including CEO Dario Amodei, collectively control 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special Class F share. No matter how many ordinary shares Anthropic sells, that voting power remains intact. A separate, independent trust, established to protect Anthropic's AI safety mission, holds Class T stock that generally lets it appoint and remove a majority of the board. Anthropic says these protections are necessary because AI is so powerful that its development must be shielded from short-term investor pressure.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  There's a more practical benefit: It's extremely difficult to oust leaders who control their company's voting power. Which brings me back to Jensen. He cofounded Nvidia 33 years ago, when it made video game chips. Back then, special voting stock was rare in tech. And claiming video games were too important to humanity to leave to ordinary shareholders would have been a tough sell. Today, Nvidia powers the AI revolution. But Huang owns only about 3.5% of its shares, without special voting rights. His board pushed him out. His supporters want him back. I suspect Jensen would do things differently if he could start again. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Jump to

E-paper has lots of applications, though it’s found a particularly solid market penetration as a replacement for simple paper price tags. Because why have a cheap slip of paper for a fraction of a cent when you could have a complicated piece of electronics displaying a price? In any case, some of these price tags can be repurposed for more interesting uses, as this work from [steanlab] demonstrates. pin16 is an open firmware for Solum EFR32BG22 e-paper price tags. Or, as the industry calls them, Electronic Shelf Labels (ESL). It covers the El016 (200×200) and EL022 (160×296) models, both of which have four colors—black, white, red, and yellow. The firmware allows uploading images over Bluetooth from a browser, turning the humble price tag into a picture frame. Pictures are converted within the browser into a format suitable for display on the tags, and are then shown as a slideshow on a timer. Updates to firmware can be made over Bluetooth once the pin16 firmware is installed, however, it’s worth noting that initial install requires using SWD to reprogram. There’s no way to backup the factory firmware either, so don’t do this on tags that don’t belong to you. They may not be the highest-resolution or prettiest digital picture frames out there, but nevertheless, it’s fun to see these tags opened up for other uses. Of course, you’re not limited to just using them as picture frames, either—you can use the firmware to upload your own tag graphics if you still want to use them as labels. We’ve seen other similar hacks before, too, and we’d love to see more—so light up the tipsline if you’ve got ’em! the savings is not in the price tag but the labor in changing it, and the frequency it can be changed eg for sales. nowadays you can always find the person a technology is meant to replace… Retail is one of the least productive forms of work. It’s added cost between getting the product from the producer to the consumer, which inflates prices without adding value to the products themselves, so the least labor and people involved in it the better it becomes for everyone. Assuming of course that the owners of the business don’t simply pocket the difference in the lack of competition, in fixed markets where only one or two big corporations command the scene.  I could see a makerspace using these for labeling. I was noticing on Temu that prices will go up after you add items to your cart hoping you won’t catch it when you pay. I can see this tactic being used by shops by remotely updating prices before you get to the cash register.  I always check my receipt after paying only to find quite often that items that were on sale were charged full price. The supermarket tactic of conveniently forgetting to update at the checkout.  Not sure if this is the same thing, but Temu advertises the “after coupon” price as the top line on every product page, using the most advantageous coupon they offer at the time, based on the item, the price,  the total price of items in your cart, and the coupon(s) which apply to the item in your cart. As you add items, the price of every item will increase or decrease based on the available automatic coupons and the mix in your basket. They may even show you the price if you increase your cart value to the next coupon up the list (10 off 50, then 15 off 75, then 25 of 100). The rack price is in smaller type, usually below the “your cost” number.  i have given up understanding the meaning of the price on temu.  but at the end of the transaction, it’s always very low :) Why do you even go to Temu?  It’s the economic version of chopping your own foot off, so you could get some disability discounts.  IIRC there were also some quiet trials of what is basically surge pricing at retail stores.  It didn’t work as well as online, but that doesn’t mean they won’t try again. Hey just think though: this could allow stores to dynamically update prices based on the tariff whims of the hour. Which is … a good… thing?  Hmmm Lower prices during low shopping hours, raise prices during rush hours.  Cause this is easier to ghange each price than, let me think… just charge a global markuo when you check out on rush hours? ;) Or just raise prices in general, and offer discounts at “off-hours” like after 8 pm. That’s what my local supermarket does. It doesn’t need dynamically updating price tags.  People with photosensitive epilepsy should stay away from these obnoxious refreshing displays. By Dade Hayes  Business Editor  	A massive AI correction wreaked more havoc on Wall Street, ending one of the worst weeks in recent memory for the stock market and erasing all of the Nasdaq‘s gains for the year.  	About $4 trillion in market value was wiped out across the AI sector, with Sandisk, Micron, Seagate, Applied Digital, Broadcom, Nvidia, Dell, AMD and Meta all taking big hits. The Nasdaq fell 1,261 points, or 5%, logging its seventh straight down day, the longest losing streak it has had since 2020.  	The Dow and the S&P 500 fared a bit better, but still slipped 2% and 4%, respectively.  	The selloff in tech coincided with two major developments in AI earlier in the week: Anthropic’s IPO and a leadership change at Nvidia.  	           			Watch on Deadline		       	After raising a record $81 billion in going public Thursday, Anthropic fell back near its $83 opening price mark. Earlier in the week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was ousted after admitting to multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy. The scandal is likely to disrupt the AI sector for some time due to pending investigations into the affair and also a complex web of investments making Nvidia not just the leading AI chipmaker but a key investor in many emerging companies.  	Against the gloomy backdrop, core Hollywood companies fared slightly better, even if it wasn’t a banner day. Disney, Skydance and Netflix all shed between 2% and 4%. Pleasure-Way has been in the RV industry for decades, to say the least, but it’s never ventured into the camping trailer form of things before. Now that it has actually taken the plunge, the American builder is ensuring that it brings to the fore a form factor that is slightly different in appearance, vivid in its color scheme, and has more customization options to suit the needs of every type of adventure seeker. The new camping trailer from the house of Pleasure-Way is called the Everbound Luxury Travel Trailer. It is an interesting take on a 21.5-foot travel trailer. The manufacturer has focused heavily on the material and quality of construction and chalked out all the details to near perfection. Whether it is to place the fiberglass body on a dual-axle trailer or slap it with a curved glass front. Designer: Pleasure-Way        The new Everbound is the company’s first caravan ever, but you don’t feel that at all by looking at its exterior and the well-fashioned interior. Inside the enticing exterior formed with a curved glass façade and plenty side windows for ample natural, you have a comfortable place to live, relax, dine and spend time. The interior is where the things get really interesting. The Everbound Luxury Travel Trailer, according to Pleasure-Way, is available in three different floor plans. You can choose from either a U-Lounge seating layout for an open and special feel inside, or if you travel with the family have a classic dinette setup by the panoramic windows. If these don’t impress you, and your family requires an entertainment area, then you can choose the entertainment lounge with a two-person loveseat facing a 43-inch LED smart TV and an electric fireplace.        Once you have selected the floor plan of your choice, you have sorted the front living space of the camping trailer. Toward the rear, you have space for sleeping, and in the middle, the kitchen and bathroom occupy the space.  The raised twin beds in the rear provide the owner with a comfortable place to settle in after the long day on the road. The company offers a choice to transform the twin beds into a king-size bed for larger sleeping space. The large windows provide plenty of natural light and provide a good view of the surrounds. The camper provides plenty of overhead storage, so that you can have all the necessary items in proximity when in bed. The galley makes practical use of the small space. You get ample cabinets below the countertop, which is occupied by a portable induction cooktop. When you’re not cooking, the cooktop can be stored away to offer space for prep and serving. The kitchen also features a 5.5 cu. ft. refrigerator, microwave, and a sink. On the opposite side of the kitchen (which is right adjacent to the entrance) is the bathroom. The bathroom is pretty spacious as well, with a 32-inch enclosed shower and a residential-style foot-flush toilet. The bathroom also has a cabinet for storage and a large opening window for ventilation.   Everbound Travel Trailer, which weighs 5,800 lb (2,631 kg), isn’t designed to be rugged or help you survive off- the-grid. Yet it comes with a 460-Ah lithium-ion battery, a 3,000-W inverter, a 500 W solar system, and a 95 L fresh water tank. You can get the trailer for a starting price of roughly $91,000. Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday. Save Share Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT). Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff. “Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds. Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent. More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep. Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fall amid tech sell-off. Save Share Asian stock markets have suffered stinging losses as fears that the AI boom is unsustainable persist despite Anthropic’s blockbuster debut. Markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell sharply on Friday, as investor excitement around the Claude creator’s public listing failed to allay concerns about the sustainability of the multitrillion-dollar investments propping up AI. Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 tumbled 5.1 percent, while Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.2 percent. In Taipei, the Taiex plunged 6.2 percent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index closed down 1.9 percent. The sell-off reflects concerns that AI-led growth is slowing down and the “peak growth phase” may have passed, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale. “The second element is on the demand vacuum that we are seeing,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera. “At the time when foreigners are not buying, it is to be seen how long can the domestic investors stay put, particularly in Korea, on which the drawdown has been more severe.” Like Wall Street, Asia’s main bourses are heavily exposed to AI. The region is home to some of the key players in the global AI ecosystem, including South Korean memory chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, Taiwanese contract chipmaker TSMC, and Japanese investment holding company SoftBank Group. Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in recent years in anticipation of future profits, stoking fears of a debt-fuelled market bubble reminiscent of the splurge that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash. Global AI-related investment is projected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner. Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at Union Bancaire Privee in Hong Kong, said the sell-off in multiple markets reflected a “collapse in confidence in the AI investment thesis”. “Global technology stocks have retreated throughout the week, with Asia’s chip-heavy markets bearing the brunt of the sell-off,” Casanova told Al Jazeera. “Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO did little to ease broader concerns about the outlook for AI-related equities and may, if anything, have crystallised the debate,” he said. “Rather than lifting the broader AI complex, the listing appears to have diverted liquidity from established AI plays as investors rotated into the new issue,” he added. “Nvidia’s earnings earlier this week also failed to provide the reassurance markets were seeking.” Market sentiment has also been dampened by moves in Washington to clamp down on China’s access to advanced chips amid claims that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese intelligence operative or asset. The United States Bureau of Industry and Security this week announced new export licence requirements aimed at preventing Chinese AI developers from remotely accessing top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in third countries, mainly in Southeast Asia. In the latest in a series of probes facing Nvidia, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on Thursday that his office had served a subpoena on the chip giant seeking information about whether its advanced chips made their way to China and whether it misled investors. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment about the probe. The market retreat in Asia followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, even as Anthropic shares jumped 17 percent on their first day of trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker “ANT.” Anthropic’s stock price opened at $111.50 before settling just above $97, vaulting the company founded less than six years ago into the ranks of the world’s most valuable firms. The San Francisco-based AI giant’s market debut came after it raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging the $75bn SpaceX initially raised in June. Despite the excitement around Anthropic, key indexes on Wall Street closed in the red, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite down 2.3 percent and the broader S&P 500 dropping 2 percent. “There are many uncertainties in the AI space currently, coupled with what many seem to believe is a questionable business model, particularly regarding ANT’s pricing power dynamics,” Kevin J Koharki, an associate professor of accounting at Purdue University, told Al Jazeera. “If these turn out to be weaker than many expect, the valuation will eventually ‘rerate’ downward,” he said. “Only time will tell.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.” In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.” Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.” As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves. Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components. When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone. Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in. “A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says. To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch. In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US. Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.” Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.” When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said. The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.” By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems. YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.” Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes. “You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.” But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].” So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile. If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life? Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies. By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.” But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people. McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, launched a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time. “I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.” Polemos Industries announced itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens. The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded. Dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he says. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Building social media apps isn’t cool anymore Big Story: Welcome to Weed Island RIP to the unloved, unwanted Cybertruck Want better search results? Tech > Services & Software > AI AI is rewriting the web in its own imperfect image, making software flaws easier to find and easier to exploit, while introducing plenty of its own imperfections. Managing Editor Managing Editor  				Edited by Jon Skillings  November 20, 2026, 8:30 am ET I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking. Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some issues. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some. Something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign,  maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.  More from CNET  Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great. “This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me. One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect. If it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers. In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.  Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention. At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse. Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it. Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.  When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.” As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.  “You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said. Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning last week.  In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram. “Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said. Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies. “The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” said Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment. AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time. The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.  It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.” And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.” The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak. That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000. “There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” said Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices. It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight. “Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said. Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.  “It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov. And patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday.  Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing issue. In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding. Big Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them? “I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase. Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says.  That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution. The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable. “I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.” Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever. “You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.” But consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a company isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection. We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. For "Grand Theft Auto 6" to become the fastest-selling entertainment property — video game or movie — of all time, publisher Take-Two Interactive Software only had to beat itself. Mission accomplished, and by a landslide. Take-Two said on Friday that the latest installment in the crime-drama series generated $3.79 billion in worldwide sales in its first day. The last game in the series, "GTA 5," rang up $1 billion in worldwide sales within three days of its 2013 release, making it the fastest-selling entertainment property at the time, per Guinness World Records. It beat Activision Blizzard's "Call of Duty: Black Ops II," which reached the milestone in 15 days in 2012, and Hollywood's then-fastest-grossing film, "The Avengers," which did so at the worldwide box office in 10 days. Now, "GTA 6," made by Take-Two's Rockstar Games studio, owns the top spot. Its predecessor had held onto the video game record all this time, while the previous movie benchmark, the 2019 Marvel release "Avengers: Endgame," reached $1 billion at the worldwide box office in five days, according to Guinness World Records. "It's a cultural event," said former longtime game-industry analyst Michael Pachter of the launch of "GTA 6" on November 19. "People are going to remember this day." The higher price tag for "GTA 6" versus its predecessor likely helped. The new standard edition costs $80, while a $100 Ultimate Edition includes premium vehicles, weapons, apparel, and other in-game content tied to the story. When "GTA 5" debuted, the standard edition retailed for $60, and a special version for $80. Early forecasts had pointed to a blockbuster launch for the new game, so the milestone isn't all that surprising. Analytics firm Newzoo estimated in July that "GTA 6" was on pace for $3.3 billion to $5.2 billion in worldwide sales by the end of its launch week, while Benchmark analyst Mike Hickey noted in August that Take-Two's fiscal 2027 guidance embedded roughly 30 million unit sales. Take-Two's fiscal year ends March 31, 2027. Workforce management tech company UKG said time-off requests for the day "GTA 6" debuted were about 20% higher than it has seen in comparable pre-Thanksgiving weeks. Some employers leaned into the frenzy. The CEO of UK-based Raptor PR gave the agency's nine employees an extra day of annual leave for the release and bought each a copy of the game. Logitech, meanwhile, offered its more than 7,000 employees an extra paid day off to play any game they choose through a new "Logi Game Day" benefit. In addition to "GTA 6," two other nostalgia-filled games debuted this month: Activision Blizzard's "World of Warcraft: Forever" and Nintendo's "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" remake. Beyond the initial rush, "GTA 6" has more sales drivers ahead. A PC version expected next year could bring another wave of buyers, while price cuts and downloadable add-on content could also keep money flowing to Take-Two. "I think people are still pricing the stock like it's a one-hit wonder," said Pachter, now managing director of strategic planning at financial-services firm Wedbush Securities. "It's not." Jump to

Taiwan's drone industry appears to be booming as the world looks for alternatives to Chinese technology, but behind the soaring export numbers is a dizzyingly messy situation that could threaten its ambitions. Taiwan has made drones a national priority, betting it can produce China-free technology more cheaply than the US or Europe to become a global drone powerhouse. On paper, the local drone industry is off to a roaring start. Drone export sales from the island known for products like semiconductors and bubble tea surged 34 times from 2024 to 2025, from 3,500 units to 122,726. By June 2026, exports had already reached 191,373. Official data shows most went to Europe. But local manufacturers and industry observers told Business Insider that Taiwan's ambitions may be being jeopardized by weak supply chain management, poor coordination, and delays in military purchases. Some question whether the export surge reflects lasting demand, while others caution that Taiwan may only have a few years to find its footing and leverage its reputation as a China-free drone maker. After that, competitors may develop their own affordable China-free supply chain solutions. "The Taiwan drone industry exists or is able to be competitive because of the split from non-Chinese drone components," said Dennis Huang, the managing director for International Strategy and Operations at drone maker Taiwan UAV. "If that didn't exist or no one cared about it, I don't think the Taiwan drone industry will be competitive at all." Chinese firms, particularly DJI, have dominated the drone market for years with their low prices, but many potential customers in the US, Europe, Middle East, and Asia wary of Chinese electronics are looking for reliable, China-free alternatives to build out their military and civilian drone arsenals. Taiwan, which vets local manufacturers supplying the military, says that it can be the kind of supplier foreign buyers are looking for. It aims to build a drone industry worth $1.5 billion by 2030, with half of its revenue from exports. The island sold $4.2 million worth of drones overseas in 2024. That figure jumped to $89 million in 2025, and in the first eight months of 2026, Taiwan exported $277 million worth of uncrewed systems, according to customs data. The problem is that those sales may not actually signal growing demand from Western militaries, a key market opportunity. Official data shows that most were smaller systems costing $800 to $1,200 each, shipped to Poland and the Czech Republic, both of which are transit points for drones bound for Ukraine, said Cathy Fang, deputy director of the national security program at the government-funded think tank Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology (DSET). At that price point, she said, these are likely FPV drones for Kyiv's war effort. Taiwan might be feeding Ukraine's enormous demand for battlefield drones, estimated at 8 million annually, rather than cornering a stable, long-term market. Taiwanese drone sales haven't been steady either. After spiking to roughly 136,000 drones exported in the first quarter of 2026, they dropped to 55,300 drones in the second quarter. Government figures don't say if these are military or civilian drones, but Fang suspects that the bulk of export sales are driven by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. "We hope that even if we don't have the war demand, maybe there will be civilian or government use to sustain it," she said. At a small Taichung factory, roughly 60 workers assemble airframes for strike and interceptor drones. The company, Carbon-Based Technology (CBT), has supplied Taiwan's military for nearly two decades. Its CEO, Stacy Yu, said that it struggled to find affordable parts when Ukraine came calling in 2022 and 2023. "Things like electric motors, batteries. Everything. Everything was very hard to find, rare and expensive," she said. That's now changed, Yu said. Hundreds of Taiwanese firms have surged into the industry as Taiwan's drone ambitions become clearer. TEDIBOA, a government-backed drone organization in Taiwan, says that roughly 290 firms on the island are now building drones or supplying manufacturers. Today, a drone maker can "find almost anything you need," said Yu. CBT's revenue hit $3.2 million in the first nine months of 2026, cutting its net losses despite remaining unprofitable. Bryce Barros, a visiting researcher with the government-funded think tank Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said Taiwan has many small- and medium-sized businesses that can quickly pivot to new opportunities. One example from July that went viral was Hocheng Corp, a ceramics company that makes toilet materials, saying it's making external armor for vehicles and is moving into drone composites. The influx of new manufacturers has exposed problems with how Taiwan's drone industry operates. Phoebe Pham, a researcher at INDSR and former RAND analyst, warned that Taiwan lacks a centralized route for manufacturers to understand military requirements and connect with government buyers. Ukraine, for example, has the Brave1 and DOT-Chain marketplaces where manufacturers can list their products, connect with one another, and see what troops need. Even in cases when Taiwanese firms managed to sell their drones to the government, the framework for getting business done is "still murky," Pham said She said military and law enforcement requirements can also become distorted as they are passed to manufacturers, potentially leading companies to develop products that don't align with what is actually needed in the field. Fang identified another weakness. Taiwan lacks uniform standards or certificates in its commercial industry to verify that its supposedly China-free drones are actually free of Chinese components. The problem has already surfaced in military procurement. In October, authorities searched the offices of Jiin Ming Industry, a Taiwanese manufacturer supplying military drones. Prosecutors alleged that CEO Alson Chien and another executive knowingly supplied drones containing prohibited Chinese-made chips and camera lenses and submitted false certificates of origin. A court ordered Chien detained for two months. The allegations have not been adjudicated. Jiin Ming told Business Insider that it was cooperating with authorities and had "consistently maintained our commitment to a non-China supply chain." The company later said it had not claimed that all of its products already met China-free requirements. The military conducts its own checks on suppliers, but the scope of its requirements is unclear to the public, Fang said. One of the reported ways that authorities caught Chinese chips in drones was simply by visually inspecting them, Fang added. "If the chip says CHN, then it's from China. But we don't have any more strict verification processes for doing that," she said of methods the industry could follow. When asked about these issues, Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said that lawmakers are establishing a drone committee to strengthen "interagency policy coordination and resource integration." The ministry said it would also develop certification standards for verifying the origins of drone parts "as soon as possible." One of the biggest hurdles Taiwan faces is that it's not buying its own drones. Large orders from Taipei for the military would give drone manufacturers confidence to invest more in workers and infrastructure, Fang said. Taiwan's military has fewer than 5,000 drones in its arsenal, according to an August assessment from Fang. The government sought $6.6 billion last year to buy some 210,000 drones by 2031, but opposition lawmakers blocked the funding for eight months. A revised $7.6 billion plan still requires annual spending approvals. That money may not start flowing until 2027, extending the delay to more than a year. The wait is costing Taiwan valuable time, Fang said, as it needs to start testing drones, collecting data, and training AI models for a market that evolves by the month. Meanwhile, the US is moving to accelerate drone purchases through its Drone Dominance program using its Blue UAS list to identify approved systems. Taiwan's procurement delays risk leaving its manufacturers behind. For Huang of Taiwan UAV, the funding dispute stalled major military tenders his company was going to bid for, including one for loitering munitions. When asked about the delay, the president's office said that it was seeking $1.7 billion this year for naval and aerial drones. A spokesperson said the administration was also looking to civilian and international markets to sustain the industry. Testing in Taiwan presents another challenge: The mountainous, densely populated island has few flat, unobstructed corridors for flying a drone. A business development manager at a US drone manufacturer said that his company established an R&D division in Taiwan, but is running prototype operations in Dubai, where the expansive desert allows larger, heavy-load drones to fly. Testing in the Middle East also allows his division to trial designs using cheaper, Chinese components. "The prototypes are all, maybe 70% China parts, except the communication module," he said. Once the US company has a flying model, it sends the schematics to its Taiwanese team, which recreates the drone using non-Chinese parts before final assembly and certification in the US. The presidential office said Taiwan is designating 18 new testing sites and seeking opportunities to test drones with international partners. Even if Taiwan resolves these problems, its biggest competitive advantage may be temporary. Huang of Taiwan UAV believes it will take about two to three years for foreign companies to develop alternatives to key components they relied on China for, such as raw materials and processing for batteries and magnets. Arvin Li, CEO of drone firm Dragonfly, estimated that Taiwan can only harness its advantage for another three to five years. "Non-China components are a right-now policy," he said, arguing that being competitive means building a competitive product. "Right now the 'non-red' supply chain will be the biggest highlight for Taiwan's drones. But in the future, if AI is embedded and with higher-end AI, you need more higher-end chips, that would be Taiwan's potential," DSET's Fang said. Richard Chou, a retired Taiwanese colonel who advocates for the local drone industry, is urging his homeland to work on software and semiconductors now. "Taiwan should avoid viewing drones as a stand-alone industry," he said. Chou, a consultant for Jiin Ming, warned that without independent certification, more scandals could undermine Taiwan's reputation at a critical moment. "The future is no longer about 'Made in Taiwan,'" Chou said. "It is about whether the world trusts Taiwan." Jump to

Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images                                       hide caption  For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term. So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures. "You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here." This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president. After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year. From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable. "Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records. Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth. Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes. Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures. In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.   A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia. Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad. For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest. "This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says. Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year. A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans. "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."                  Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, is set to become chair of the House Oversight Committee in January.                                                           Mark Schiefelbein/AP                                       hide caption  But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election. Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024. The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial. Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company. The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector. Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power. Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures. "I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat. But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion. World Liberty Financial declined to comment.                  A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bought a major stake in World Liberty Financial.                                                           Vahid Salemi/AP                                       hide caption  Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits. Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year. The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market. Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month. Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times. While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits. "Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment. But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. It was another beautiful day for Wall Street—and a nerve-racking one for anyone already nervous about how much the United States’ economy is intertwined with the A.I. bubble. On Thursday morning, siblings and Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the bell at the Nasdaq to launch the initial public offering for their monumentally valued tech firm, with shares originally priced at a whopping $83 each. Even before $ANT opened up to the public, early investors in the company helped bring in an unprecedented $81 billion haul. Once the stock did go on wider sale, however, it hit a peak of $111.50 a share for a $2 trillion valuation, before falling a touch as the day went on, still trading high yet settling below the $100 threshold. Meanwhile, by the markets’ close, overall Nasdaq values fell slightly, by 2 percent.  Anthropic has already smashed the historic records SpaceX set when it hit the indexes earlier this year—and thus is counterintuitively putting itself up for more scrutiny and already-visible panic. Much like Elon Musk’s rockets-and-A.I. firm, Anthropic is selling a vision of an extremely speculative future and almost zero executive accountability, while carrying alarming losses on its balance sheets and wiggling its way into the stock indexes with more than a little help from regulation exemptions as well as your retirement accounts. The maker of Claude Code is also springing forward with this IPO in a moment when the A.I. boom has never felt more fragile. Thursday is no doubt a historic triumph for Anthropic, but it’s one with little promise that the good times will continue. Let’s look at some numbers. Anthropic’s revenue has grown this year, but at a slower pace than before, and its monetary gains don’t even clear $1 billion. At the same time, its losses and steepest obligations have ballooned: The company has nearly $1 trillion worth of chips and computing deals with corporations like Amazon, Google, and Nvidia up through 2030—and $70 billion of that comes due within the next 10 months. Yes, the public investment bonanza will help, but Anthropic’s paths to growth and ability to pad its profit margins are already facing a limit. Bloomberg’s chief U.S. economist, Anna Wong, pointed out that the firm is no longer able to price its tokens at as premium a level as it was able to do in the past, squeezing one area of further growth. (So much for “tokenmaxxing.”) And where Anthropic’s business stands to go from here puts a lot of people beyond Big Tech on the hook. With 401(k)s and pension funds indubitably exposed to the Nasdaq, it should concern everyone that an index already battered by A.I. bearishness couldn’t lift itself up even via the largest IPO in history. (And other indexes fared even worse yesterday.) In the wake of the stock market bearishness fueled by the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—a fall in the chipmaker’s fortunes that has not bounced back in spite of Nvidia’s impressive numbers this past quarter—the people with the most to lose from a broader market rout are rightfully fearful. On Thursday morning, a few dozen protesters gathered outside the Nasdaq, some of whom were arrested in the process; one of the leading organizers told Mother Jones that the IPO frenzy reminded him of the ultraconcentration that fueled 2008’s market bust and the Great Recession. (Last month, New York City’s comptroller wrote to Anthropic asking it to pause the IPO until major risks around A.I. capabilities and finances were addressed, to no avail.) AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler wrote in a statement that “worker pension plans and 401(k) accounts will absorb Anthropic shares whether they choose to invest in the company or not,” exposing its members to “increasing risks to our financial markets and workers’ retirement security.” Shuler also made a grim 2008 analogy, insisting that “we cannot make the same mistake with unregulated AI” that the financial sector did with unregulated debt swaps. One only need look at Anthropic rival SpaceX as a sign of what may come: The IPO that initially hit a peak of $200 is now down by nearly 10 percent of its asking price. It’s still riding high, to be sure, but at nowhere near as robust a level as once promised. (Musk, who just expressed his regret at wasting hundreds of millions of dollars backing MAGA midterms candidates, hasn’t even been a trillionaire for a few months now. Sad!) As for the other tech stocks that once catapulted off A.I. hype? They are also crashing, whether they are A.I. “neoclouds” or Big Tech giants who look to A.I. as just one part—if still a major part—of their business. The Amodei siblings may have been smiling on Wall Street this week, but people at all class levels are not feeling so much exuberance right now. Anthropic, overall, has been enjoying the ride and will probably do so for a little while yet. But at some point, the lofty promises will need to be cashed. And some of the buyers who expressed their confidence will likely cash out themselves before Anthropic sees earth again. Slate is published by The Slate           Group, a Graham Holdings Company.
