In regulated markets like healthcare, a working product isn’t enough — startups must also figure out who pays, how adoption happens, and what to prove before scaling.   		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.    Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.    The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.    Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.    Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.    Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?    Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other.   Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an important regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.    As an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off.   This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets. Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction.   A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.    Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.    Has the founder or company addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.                     These challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly important. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.    At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.    That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.    AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.    The traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.    Moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.    For investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.    The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense. For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.    Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.    The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.     We'll be in your inbox every morning Monday-Saturday with all the day’s top business news, inspiring stories, best advice and exclusive reporting from Entrepreneur.

Google slipped to 6% (from 7%), though that's double its 3% share in Q2, thanks to the launch of the Pixel 11 series. Everyone else combined accounted for just 3% of US shipments in Q3, down from 7% a year ago. So the Apple-Samsung-Motorola-Google quadropoly is only getting stronger. Experts say Trump administration is not taking the threat of AI attacks seriously, as consumers stock up on supplies. Save Share Consumers in the United States have dealt with a number of technology-related outages in the last week, affecting services provided by major banks and companies such as Microsoft, Workday, and Apple. Even the US government has experienced problems, including a national aviation ground stop and an ongoing problem affecting the internal network at the country’s premier surveillance agency. US officials have downplayed suggestions that the incidents are related. “Tell them to relax, everything is good, these are individual events,” US President Donald Trump told a reporter on Fox on Thursday when asked about the outages and whether the public should be preparing for emergencies. The White House fired the US cybersecurity chief on Thursday and appointed a replacement, days after the disruptions. US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in media interviews on Wednesday that the outages likely stemmed from organisations using artificial intelligence (AI) to fix security flaws and carry out maintenance updates. The tech outages come after months of public alarm over the threat posed by AI, as well as messaging by governments in the US and other countries about other events that has inadvertently added to that concern. In the UK, Sweden, and Japan, for example, authorities have run campaigns in recent months to remind the public to store essentials at home such as torches, water, and medicine, in case they experience stronger-than-usual storms this winter due to the El Nino phenomenon. Last month, the US Department of Defense announced it was rolling out a programme to ensure all military bases could operate for 90 days without relying on the civilian power grid. “It’s been an unusual stretch. People have had problems with several services they rely on in their daily lives, and we’re still learning what happened in some of these cases,” said Danny Atherton, a lecturer at Georgetown University and editor of the AI Incident Database, which tracks global outages and attacks reported to have involved the use of AI. “I worry most about essential services,” Atherton said. “If a shared system goes down, can a hospital still take care of patients? … I think governments and AI providers should expect serious outages to continue.” More and more companies are using AI to test their systems and finding vulnerabilities that could potentially be exploited by malicious actors in unexpected ways. Last month, the FBI said cybercriminals linked to the North Korean government were able to steal $6bn in cryptocurrency from the Binance crypto exchange. The hackers reportedly used AI in several parts of the complex operation, posing as recruiters from another company to conduct video interviews with engineers, planting malicious software on their computers, and eventually gaining access to crypto wallets holding the funds. Peter Slattery, a research scientist at MIT’s FutureTech, said the Binance heist is one example of how AI might have played a role in the series of outages in recent weeks, but may not yet have been noticed. Malicious actors could have used AI to conduct research, or create deepfakes that were convincing enough to win the trust of key employees at target companies. Software may have been updated to accommodate AI tools, or it might have recommended changes to how a company operates that turned out to be problematic. “We are moving into an era where AI is increasingly useful, both for hacking and for a variety of other tools,” Slattery told Al Jazeera. “It’s quite likely, but not guaranteed, that things will get worse. We will have more attacks from AI on infrastructure, and there will be some significant attacks and harmful events over the next year or two.” Slattery points out that companies are already seeking to insulate themselves from liability if a potential AI-powered attack happens. In the last few months, for instance, several major banks, including JP Morgan, Citibank, and Bank of America, have notified customers that if they use third-party tools that use AI to access their accounts, the banks will not be liable for any losses if something goes wrong. The speed with which Trump administration officials have brushed off questions about the threat posed by recent outages has also reduced confidence among experts, like Deanne Criswell, who served as the head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) until 2025. “We can’t just take the first answers as the absolute answers, because sometimes these vulnerabilities can be buried deep within the system, and we have to do our due diligence to understand the cause,” Criswell told Al Jazeera. She said that incidents like the airline ground stop last week should not be treated in the same way as natural disasters. After a hurricane, FEMA officials can fairly quickly assess the damage, and estimate how long it would take to restore critical services, whether that is days, or weeks, or even months later. “But in a cyber or tech-related incident, I don’t know that, I’m not an expert in that, and I have to bring in those outside partners … to help us better understand the cause,” Criswell explained. FEMA relied on the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to do that, Criswell said, but it is unclear what the impact of budget and staff cuts has been at the agency under Trump. The agency is tasked with maintaining contact with the myriad of private companies that control everything from water to power and telecommunications in the US. More than a third of its staff were lost to cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in 2025, and in the administration’s proposed budget for 2027, CISA would face $700m in cuts. The measures demonstrate “a dangerous underestimation of the threats facing our nation from adversaries and criminals who seek to destabilise our national security, economy, public health, and safety”, Democratic Senator Mark Warner of the state of Virginia wrote to the agency in June. Regardless of official messaging, or what might actually be to blame for the incidents, they are not going unnoticed by the US public, said Chris Ellis, a disaster preparedness expert and Director of Education and Strategic Outreach for The American Civil Defense Association. More and more people in the US have sought to collect supplies such as food, water, and other essentials in recent years, especially after moments of crisis, like the outbreak of the Ukraine war, or the global pandemic. After each election, Ellis says, the losing side in the US has also tended to purchase emergency supplies. In 2024, more than 20 million Americans had enough supplies to last them 31 days or longer after a disaster, according to Ellis – a number that has grown in recent years and months. Regardless of government efforts to calm public fears, Ellis says the proportion of people who are actively preparing for a disaster is reaching the point where the practice might be normalised, as it was in previous generations, or still is in some other countries. “We are kind of at that stage where prepping is still seen as fringe, but not crazy,” he said. Spencer Platt/Getty Images                                       hide caption  President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans. Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately. Loading... In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process. While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt. "There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party." Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests. But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass. "It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap." The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics. On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action. Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses. "Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?" But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results. "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online. The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much." "There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns." To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust. "It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said. But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026. The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab. Wall Street is staring at a sea of red in tech and AI names since the market climbed to all-time highs barely a month ago. A bruising weekslong sell-off in tech stocks sent the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year on Friday, while dragging the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction.  Now, more Wall Street forecasters are posing a tough question for investors: is the AI trade over? Concerns about the end of the artificial intelligence-fueled bull market have picked up amid the bloodbath in the tech sector. Selling has been driven by panic about slowing AI capex, the "blunami" midterms and the impact on data centers, and the Nvidia crisis that's now taken the stock down by 47% since early October. Most recently, Anthropic's IPO came and went without making a positive impact on the broader market. The record public offering was expected to give the AI sector a much-needed boost, and the market's mixed reaction is the latest evidence that the AI trade is struggling. The Nasdaq 100 is inching closer to an official bear market. The tech-heavy index is down 17% from its all-time high earlier this year, but many corners of the tech sector are already in bear territory. More painful losses are being felt in the chips, memory, data center, and neocloud sectors. Wells Fargo is flagging the risk of a broader valuations reset in the AI space, the bank wrote this week, triggered by factors like higher rates, elevated oil prices, signs of economic weakness, and tighter regulation of AI, Sameer Samana, the head of global equities and real assets at the bank, told Business Insider. Samana said the market's reaction to this week's mega-IPO from Anthropic supported the bank's view that the AI sector could be in the midst of a reset. He declined to give an estimate of how much stock prices could fall, but laid out one hypothetical where earnings growth cratered by 33%, leading valuations to fall in suit. "The IPO is sucking a lot of liquidity from other parts of the market," he said, adding that the bank favored large-cap communication services, industrials, and materials stocks to avoid becoming "overly reliant on the AI story." "We expect volatility to remain elevated as markets reassess AI spending, regulation, industry leadership, and the conversion of investment into free cash flow," the note added. With Anthropic's IPO in the rearview, investors are turning their attention back toward AI capex, with many wondering if spending will continue to hold up and justify mega valuations in the tech space. A major fear brewing is that data center spending will slow in the next year as lawmakers crack down on new construction, capping growth in the sector. Investment research firm TS Lombard said it changed its stance on global equities to "underweight," trimming areas exposed to AI in the US and Taiwan. The firm added that it is "sceptical" of the idea that the market can avoid an AI crash altogether, and in a separate note, it laid out a scenario where the market sees a "definite vibe shift" by the end of 2027, resulting in a 40% crash in AI-linked stocks by early 2028 as tech firms slash capex guidance. "The question was whether AI could generate the massive, unprecedented revenues that could justify those multi-trillion-dollar investments, particularly when the underlying tech was now freely available and most regular people just weren't that fussed. By early 2028, the answer to that question was a resounding 'no,'" strategists wrote of their hypothetical scenario. Capital Economics, a research firm that has long warned of an AI bubble, pointing to the risks around AI revenue and investment. The firm predicted the S&P 500 dropping 9% through the end of next year in a note following Anthropic's IPO, though the index could post even steeper losses in the interim. "The revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding. And a combination of the other risks, even in minor form, looks plausible: for example, somewhat stricter regulation of the buildout and application of AI, plus a tightening of AI-related financing," researchers wrote. "A stock market AI bust in 2027 has long been our central forecast and appears to be a growing concern for investors," the firm added. Citi said it cut its risk exposure to US equities last month and, in a note this week, advised investors to remain on guard. The bank highlighted spillover risks related to Nvidia, given that the chip giant backstops a wide range of data center projects, neocloud providers, and AI firms. Jensen Huang's departure is also being viewed by some investors as a nearly existential risk, given that Huang served as the unofficial poster child of the AI trade. "AI risks have been rising," analysts wrote, adding that the rotation in stocks recently resembled the "extreme" moves leading up to the burst of the dot-com bubble. Others are taking issue with the sheer magnitude of tech's decline from record highs. The prominent AI researcher Gary Marcus pointed to losses all over the tech sector in his newsletter, Marcus on AI, on Friday. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF, for instance, is down 24% from its summertime peak. "In the coming months (if not days) Nvidia and the Neoclouds will get hit hard," Marcus wrote in a note on Substack. "It is very much looking like the death spiral that this newsletter has long warned about has begun." Jump to

Tech > Mobile > Mobile Accessories Polaroid’s little photo printer helps me quickly save memories with superb photo quality. Writer Writer  				Edited by Mike Sorrentino  November 20, 2026, 8:00 am ET I loved journaling as a child. It helped me survive hormonal changes, the usual teen dramas, plus a hefty dose of existential angst. Then college called, and I moved to a different country, leaving behind my childhood, my Nirvana cassettes (I’m old, OK?) and, sadly, my journaling habit. I made multiple attempts to return to journaling throughout the years, with varying success. I’ve delved into bullet journals under the pretense of improving my productivity, but I gave up when it became too much effort. I’ve invested in multiple notebooks and planners, only to eventually neglect them.  Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer.  More from CNET It all began when I discovered the wondrous world of journaling TikTok. In short-form videos, creators would show off beautiful journal pages decorated with colored markers, stickers, washi tape and, yes, photos — specifically photos from portable printers because the prints are small enough to fit within the confines of a typical journal or planner. I really liked the idea of decking out my journal pages with photos of my everyday life. I knew I had to get one.  After a bit of research, I decided on a couple of criteria. First, I wanted the printer to be a dye sublimation printer rather than a ZINK (Zero Ink) printer. Dye sublimation printers essentially use heat to transfer dye onto the paper, while ZINK printers use a special paper that activates under heat with no ink required (hence the name). Dye sublimation prints tend to be higher quality because it transfers the dye in layers of cyan, magenta and yellow, followed by a protective coating.  Second, I wanted the photo to be on sticky paper so that I didn’t have to mess around with glue to add these photos to my journal.  I found quite a number of dye sublimation pocket printers on the market, but the one that caught my eye immediately was the Polaroid Hi-Print 2×3 Generation 2 pocket printer. I fell in love with it the moment I saw it. The sleek white design, the Polaroid logo and that curved rainbow accent on the edge really sealed the deal for me. Call me a sucker for style, I guess. I purchased a Hi-Print 2×3 “starter set,” which includes the printer along with two 2×3 paper cartridges. Each cartridge has 10 photo sheets, and each sheet is made out of sticky back photo paper, which is exactly what I wanted. Both the Gen 2 and the prior Gen 1 are easy to find; the main difference is the newer one uses a USB-C charging port while the original uses the older Micro-USB port. Getting started with the printer is simple enough: Download the Polaroid Hi-Print app, pair the printer with your phone and you’re ready to go. The app is fairly easy to navigate. I like that it lets you arrange your photos in collages so you’re not limited to just one photo per sheet. You can also decorate your prints with colorful frames or decorations. The printer even offers a mosaic option that lets you print out one big image using multiple sheets.  Since it’s a dye sublimation printer, the Hi-Print prints out photos in stages. It lays down the different colors in multiple passes (yellow in the first pass, magenta in the second pass, and so forth). Because of that, printing does take a while: around 60 seconds per photo.  But I don’t mind the delay, as the resulting photo quality is superb. The colors are vibrant and the overall image is nice and sharp. The contrast could be a little better, but for a little pocket printer, the quality definitely exceeded my expectations.  There are a few downsides, however. The obvious one is that photo cartridges can be pretty expensive. One pack of 20 sheets is around $17, though you can get it for $14 each if you buy the 5-pack. That’s still almost 70 cents per 2×3 print. If you use multiple prints, that can add up pretty quickly.  Another downside is that it doesn’t have a super long battery life. It only has a 620mAh battery, which Polaroid says will last up to 20 photo printing sessions. I only ever use this printer at home, so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I can see this being a potential disappointment if you want to bring this printer on the road. That said, if you do want to charge it, it doesn’t take that long. Polaroid says it takes under an hour, and that feels about right based on my experience.  I’ve had this printer for a few months now, and I’m very pleased with it. Since I use the photos primarily with my journal, I also really appreciate how thin the photo sheets are, so they don’t bulk up the pages too much. I truly enjoy printing out my little creations, cutting out my collages and then decorating my journal with them.  I might not have my childhood back nor my Nirvana cassettes, but at least I’ve finally recaptured the joys of journaling — even if it did require a bit of help from a pocket printer.   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. When thinking about a winter getaway, many travelers likely imagine either a snow-covered mountain town or a warm, tropical destination. After visiting all 50 states, though, I've found that my favorite destinations generally fall somewhere in between. For instance, Charleston, South Carolina, might not be the first place you think of when booking a winter getaway, but in my opinion, it's well worth the trip. Unlike more traditional winter destinations like Aspen or Stowe, Charleston doesn't revolve around snow or skiing. It also doesn't have the heat of a tropical beach destination. However, the mild winter means I can enjoy plenty of time outside. With average highs in the 60s and lows around 40 degrees Fahrenheit from December through February, I feel like I get the best of both worlds — and it's part of the reason why I keep going back. I love being able to grab a coffee and stroll through the historic downtown and French Quarter in the morning, enjoy a patio lunch or happy hour in the afternoon, and even walk along a nearby beach in just a light jacket. Hospitality is a major part of Charleston's economy, with tourists visiting in large numbers year-round. But if, like me, you enjoy a more peaceful winter getaway, the offseason is where you'll find the fewest crowds. Especially after the holidays, I've found the city is quieter for a month or two before spring festivals and higher tourism begin again. Luckily, though, there's still plenty to do in the cooler months. The holiday season brings many street fairs and special events, and the popular Southeastern Wildlife Exposition and Lowcountry Oyster Festival — which are both on my Charleston bucket list — take place in February. For me, one of the best parts of traveling in the winter offseason has been the chance to stay at some of the area's high-end, luxury hotels for a fraction of what they might cost during peak season. Some hotels even offer discounted rates and complimentary upgrades during the cooler months. During my last visit in December, I was able to combine lower rates with my American Express Platinum Card hotel credit to stay at The Dewberry — a luxury property right downtown — for less than half of what I'd pay during other seasons. There's something magical about the holiday season in Charleston. My last visit was about a week before Christmas, and I loved spending my days walking around the extravagantly decorated homes on the Battery, wandering through the American Gardens Holiday Market, and strolling King Street to browse shops for holiday gifts. I especially love that I don't need an itinerary to enjoy Charleston — during any season. Some of my favorite moments have been simply wandering the historic streets, taking in the decorations, and stopping into shops wherever something caught my eye. One of the things I love most about visiting Charleston in the winter is that the coast feels completely different from the busy summer months. Several beautiful beaches are within driving distance of downtown, and in the winter, I can often walk for long stretches without seeing many other people. Edisto Beach, Isle of Palms, Folly Beach, and Kiawah Island are a few of my favorites, each with its own personality. Although it might not be swimming weather, I love taking a long walk along the shoreline, watching the waves, and enjoying the kind of peace and quiet you rarely find at these beaches during peak season. The shorter days also make it easier to catch a sunrise or sunset along the coast before heading into town for dinner at one of Charleston's seafood restaurants. Jump to

For more than 25 years, I worked in film, eventually running production at companies for Ridley Scott, Tony Scott, Barry Sonnenfeld, and Luc Besson. I had a career I was proud of, a beautiful Los Angeles house, and the professional life I'd worked decades to build. For much of that time, success meant the next promotion, a bigger salary, a bigger house, and more responsibility. I loved my work. I loved making movies, solving creative problems with smart people, and mentoring younger executives. When it was good, it was great. I didn't particularly want to leave Hollywood. I wanted more control over my life. By 2021, the company I worked for was running out of money, and I knew my job was ending. After decades in a business where the demands were relentless, and someone else controlled my schedule, I wondered what I wanted next. My husband and I had also begun exploring an idea we'd talked about for years: moving to Italy. I'd traveled to 67 countries, and Italy was the place I kept returning to. The year before, we'd looked at property, imagining a vacation home and perhaps moving there someday. Then we examined the economics. We owned a five-bedroom 1911 Craftsman house in Los Angeles that we loved and couldn't imagine selling. But we could rent it out. We could live somewhere smaller. Healthcare in Italy would cost dramatically less. We wouldn't have a mortgage there. We realized we didn't need to replicate our Los Angeles income to live well. That was the turning point. I'd spent decades assuming that earning more money was the way to buy freedom. It finally occurred to me that needing less might accomplish the same thing. In August 2021, my husband and I went to LAX with an enormous pile of luggage and our equally enormous dog, Grueby, and our cat, Limbert. I hadn't announced that I was leaving Hollywood. I was still working remotely when we arrived in Italy, and when colleagues asked when I was coming back, I said I was taking it one month at a time. I didn't know whether we'd last a year. There was nothing particularly la dolce vita about what happened next. Speaking Italian was urgent, so we enrolled in language school for four hours a day, five days a week, learning from scratch. We did that for six months. We discovered how much accumulated knowledge you lose by moving countries. In the US, I knew all the little life hacks: paying a bill, filling a prescription, getting something fixed, making an appointment. Suddenly, I didn't know how to do anything. And downsizing was harder than I expected. Our Los Angeles house was filled with Arts and Crafts furniture we'd collected over the years. We had separate offices, a gym, a movie theater, a yard, and a beautiful kitchen my husband had just finished building. Our Rome apartment has one bedroom and one bathroom. There are two couches in the living room, and that's pretty much our world. I haven't discovered that possessions are meaningless. I miss some of mine. I miss walking barefoot in my backyard. I miss having a desk with a computer on it. I kind of miss my Emmy statue. But I don't miss having nearly every hour of my life spoken for. Now I can wrap a morning around seeing a single painting. I shop for whatever looks good at my neighborhood market and decide what we're eating that day. If I want to spend two hours making dinner, I can. Last month, I woke up to beautiful weather and decided to go to Umbria for a few days. Oddly, this life also requires more face-to-face interaction. Things I once did online involve a trip to the pharmacy, tabaccheria, or post office and a conversation with an actual human being. Sometimes I love it. Sometimes I would kill for a functioning website. I haven't stopped working. I continue to develop film projects, and I'd happily leave Italy for several months to produce the right movie. I miss having a team and the satisfaction of smart people trying to make something together. What has changed is the bargain I'm willing to make. I still want to make movies. I still want to work with talented people and be part of something ambitious. But I no longer want a career that requires me to surrender control over my time in pursuit of the next professional achievement. I gave up income, space, convenience, and parts of a working life I genuinely loved. In exchange, I got something I hadn't realized was so valuable until I had it: the ability to decide what to do with my own day. Jump to

Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis. Levent AlpÃ¶ge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem. If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater". The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades. As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude. It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is. Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line. Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact. AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery. "The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier." "I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added. The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long. Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off. "I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said. No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI. OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move. More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise. The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems. Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.  A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics". "We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter. A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems. It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity. The Siza Award is an annual architecture prize established by the Serralves Foundation to honor socially responsible design and public architecture. It places special emphasis on architectural generosity and targets emerging practices and architects in their thirties and forties with demonstrated sensitivity to local communities, territory, and the environment. The recognition is grounded in the conviction, reflected in Siza's career, that architects are agents of change with the ability to influence democratic discourse, whether in rebuilding urban identities or promoting social inclusion. As stated by the Foundation, the new generation of architects it targets now faces the challenge "to bridge the gap between human scarcity and technological advancement, rethinking the rules of the game and exploring archetypes, materials, shelters, labor, and other ways of improving life as a whole." The latest quarterly data for the US smartphone market reveals that Google Pixel is holding its ground despite the overall market faltering, and the other two major Android brands struggling. The top smartphone brands in the United States include Apple, Samsung, Motorola, and Google Pixel in that order. Apple continues to absolutely dominate at a whopping 57% market share in Q3 2026, up from 50% during the same period last year. Samsung came in at 25%, up 1% from last year (likely driven by a very successful Fold 8 launch during Q3), while Motorola shrank from 12% to 8%.  Google Pixel made up 6%, down 1% from Q3 2025, Counterpoint Research shows. Q3 is important for Google as it includes the company’s new August release window for new flagships. It’s not surprising that Google dropped a percentage point year-over-year, as the company’s Pixel 11 launch was not particularly exciting, especially as prices rose over the previous generation. If anything, only dropping 1% must be pretty encouraging given the overall market conditions and RAMageddon of it all. Something to note – Google Pixel is technically growing this year compared to last. Just out of view on this latest update, Q2 2026 saw Google’s share up 1% year-over-year, and Q1 was also up compared to the same period in 2025. For You Settings  news Alerts There are no new alerts at this time Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy. The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts.  “Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday.  Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses.  Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook. The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation.  “In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday. Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout.  This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples.  Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings.  While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations.  Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share. Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals. Seth Wenig/AP                                       hide caption  NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. "The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over." Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Published Nov 19, 2026 at 11:26 PM EST News Editor Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and incoming Florida governor, said that 2028 hopefuls will need to redefine their own coalitions and not recreate the previous administrations.  “To be blunt: What I’ve observed in politics, it’s very hard for somebody to try to recreate the previous person’s coalition,” Donalds told Politico at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in part on Thursday.  Donalds made history as Florida's first Black governor to be elected to office. President Donald Trump threw his support behind Donalds as did Florida Governor Ron DeSantis after the primary.  Following devastating midterm election losses for Republicans, which resulted in losing both House and Senate majority, speculation has swirled surrounding who will be the successor to MAGA after Trump is out of office.  DeSantis' post-midterm media rounds have sparked intrigue into whether he is considering another bid for the White House. He was asked about a potential 2028 run by CNN's Jake Tapper after Election Day and said in part that he has not "planned anything."  Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Glenn Youngkin, former Republican governor of Virginia, and many more have all been asked about their intentions for running in 2028 on the Republican side. Similarly, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and many more have also been asked about their political futures on the Democratic side.  During his conversation with Politico's Adam Wren, Donalds said that “Whoever the next person is going to be, they’re going to have to — in some respects — redefine and reshape the electorate about what their supportive coalition is.“ "I think trying to go back into trying to recreate what somebody else’s success was, I think is foolhardy,” he added. Donalds was asked by Politico if his comments were aimed at Vance, and he responded in part that it is "just the reality of politics,” and running on someone else's coalition "rarely works." “I would advise anybody who’s thinking about taking the next step: You got to define yourself,” Donalds also told the outlet on Thursday. “You have to be yourself. You can’t be a facsimile or a carbon copy or shades of gray of somebody else.” Following the midterm losses, Trump administration officials speculated on why the results unfolded in such a bruising manner. Vance said that after speaking with a pollster, four areas jumped out, including ending the war with Iran, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing America's relationship with Israel. Trump was asked if he had spoken with Vance about 2028 after the midterms and said in part earlier this month, "We'll see what happens. ... You don't know who's talking about running. ... Maybe he won't run, I don't know who's gonna run." Last month, Vance said he thought the president would endorse him should he launch an official 2028 campaign but added they had not discussed it. Donalds also shot down any potential 2028 run for himself saying to Politico that he is "absolutely" shutting the door on it, adding "it is not happening." “I take this job very seriously,” he later added. “I am not looking at another one.” Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Thursday, "Donalds is saying the obvious out loud. Coalitions are personal. Trump’s is built around him. [Former President Barack] Obama’s was built around him. Trying to photocopy either one usually fails. The next Republican nominee will have to assemble something that fits their own strengths and the electorate of 2028, not 2024. That is basic politics, not a break with Trump. "His quick no on running himself is also practical. He just won Florida. He has a full term ahead, a legislature to manage, and a record to build. Jumping into a national primary before he has governed would look premature to most voters and donors," Agranoff added. "It keeps the focus on the job he just got and leaves the 2028 field open for others who are already positioning. It is the kind of clear answer that avoids speculation without creating new problems." On prediction market Kalshi Thursday night, Vance has a 33 percent chance of winning the GOP presidential nomination. Rubio has 22 percent and DeSantis has 16 percent. On Polymarket, Vance has 33 percent Thursday night, Rubio has 21 percent, DeSantis has 15 percent and other potential candidates, including Cruz, Youngkin and Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, all have single digits. Anthropic’s stock fell eight percent as the market opened Friday, extending a slide that has wiped out much of the gains from its market debut. Anthropic shares are down about 22 percent from their IPO high, and the overall AI industry is struggling as well. MarketWatch reports that shares of Anthropic traded at $88.82 Friday morning, down from Thursday’s high price of $114.99 and not far above the company’s $83 IPO price. Anthropic had closed Thursday with a $1.29 trillion valuation, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Friday’s premarket levels would put that figure closer to $1.16 trillion. The slide wasn’t isolated. AI-linked stocks were broadly lower Friday: Sandisk dropped 18.24 percent, Nebius Group fell 9.39 percent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 7.72 percent, among many others. Major indexes fell too. The Dow was down 2.19 percent, the S&P 500 off 2.02 percent, the Nasdaq down 2.25 percent. The VIX, a measure of market volatility, jumped 8.93 percent. The 10 year Treasury yield stood at 4.979 percent, while crude oil fell 1.03 percent, gold dropped 3.19 percent and bitcoin slipped 0.99 percent. Jeffrey Favuzza, a trading desk analyst at Jefferies, linked the broader tech pullback to Anthropic’s struggles in a note to clients. “The vast majority of this continued selling pressure in the last 24 hours feels more to do with” Anthropic’s inability to hold its opening price, he wrote, adding that the move is being read as “bad for the rest of tech.” Only one other IPO since 1990 has surged on its debut while the broader market was falling, according to a related report. Two Wall Street firms initiated coverage of Anthropic after Thursday’s close, and they landed in different places. Seaport Research’s Jay Goldberg started the stock at neutral, writing that he is “cautious, not negative” on what he called an “incredible company.” Still, he said the IPO is “asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors” and that “we think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very big questions about its growth trajectory.” Goldberg pointed to Anthropic’s revenue growth, which slowed to 43 percent from the second to third quarter after climbing 144 percent from the first to second quarter. He called that deceleration “worrying” and said “to merit its valuation, it will need to see much higher growth rates over the next two years.” William Blair’s Arjun Bhatia took the opposite view. He initiated coverage with an outperform rating and described Anthropic as a “generational company driving a generational technology shift.” He acknowledged the unresolved risks that Goldberg flagged, saying “questions about the future are worth asking, even those that don’t have an answer at this point,” but cautioned against weighing them too heavily, adding that his team doesn’t “want to miss the forest for the trees.” Bhatia framed Anthropic’s position within the broader AI boom in sweeping terms: “We think AI is a generational shift in the tech landscape, and Anthropic is leading the charge in developing AI with a select handful of other companies.” He also predicted the company’s influence would keep expanding, saying “over the next decade, we think Anthropic is only going to become more important and consume a greater portion of enterprise spend.” AI giants like Anthropic simultaneously release powerful AI models and call for industry regulation. This video can not be played Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago. The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development. Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth. "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said. "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability." Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued. Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices. Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record. But tech stocks more broadly also fell. Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls. Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit. Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower. Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses. Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990. Known best for camper vans and small motorhomes, Pleasure-Way has been a North American RV market staple for 40 years. But until this year, it's never tried its hand at a camping trailer. That changes in a major way with the Everbound Luxury Travel Trailer, which might just be one of the nicest 20-foot+ travel trailers to debut this year. Clearly, the company's experience in the motorized end of the market translates nicely into towables.  Pleasure-Way creates a classic dual-axle travel trailer silhouette that stands out from the pack thanks to just the right amount of curve up front. The large window bear-hugging the arched fiberglass further enhances things and makes you want to step inside to enjoy the panorama from the comfort of cushion.  With that little bit of flair up front (accentuated by available two-tone paint options), Pleasure-Way is free to straighten the alu-framed bonded fiberglass out down the remainder of the cabin, using a simple, boxy design to maximize interior living space. The rows of windows along the sidewalls ensure the curvaceous front pane isn't alone in creating sweeping views of the trailer's surrounds.  While the Everbound's exterior is a step or two up from the typical white trailer box, it's the interior that really shines and shows off Pleasure-Way's decades of experience in motorhome design. Optimized around two people but able to sleep four comfortably, the trailer features a rear master bed/front dinette layout. The bedroom is centered around a raised pair of 75 x 30-in (191 x 76-cm) twin beds, each flanked by a wide-view window. Those beds can then be combined into a 75 x 80-in (191 x 203-cm) king. A command touchscreen mounted on the wall between the two twin beds provides convenient control of onboard amenities from the comfort of bed. Overhead side cabinets, a 24-in TV on the front wall and individual reading lights complete the cozy space.  As for the front dinette, Pleasure-Way offers three different options. The first is a single-bench "entertainment lounge" anchored by a two-seat bench facing the far sidewall. This version includes a 43-in LED TV hanging above an electric fireplace. Users sit behind the removable dining table and enjoy watching TV while eating or can swap the table out for a footrest to create an L-shaped chaise lounge.  The dinette can also be specced in a vis-a-vis two-bench layout or in a wraparound-sofa design. Pleasure-Way doesn't mention convertible bed kit options on the wraparound sofa or entertainment lounge setups but confirms the classic vis-a-vis dinette can convert over into a double bed to boost total sleeping capacity to four. The fireplace and 43-in TV are exclusive to the entertainment lounge floor plan.  Moving back, the sidewall opposite the entry door houses a 156-L fridge, convenient to both the dinette and galley across the way.  Next to the fridge, the dry bathroom includes a closed corner shower with handheld sprayer, a vanity with Corian countertop and sink, and a foot-flush ceramic bowl toilet. There's also a window with privacy shade and two cabinets.  Across the aisle, the kitchen block comes topped in Corian and freed of clutter by a portable induction cooker that stows away when not in use. It also includes a large rectangular sink with tall pull-out Moen faucet and cover, an under-counter microwave, and plenty of storage overhead and down low.  The Everbound isn't exactly a rugged off-grid machine, but it does come wired with plenty of power via a 460-Ah lithium-ion battery with internal heating system, Xantrex 3,000-W inverter, 500-W solar charging package and 100-A charger. It also includes a 30-A shore power hookup, 11,500-BTU Truma VarioHeat furnace, Truma instant water heater and 13,500-BTU Truma air conditioner. A 95-L tank carries fresh water and an outdoor quick-connect LP hookup makes for easy grill connection.  The 21.5-foot (6.5-m) Everbound tips the scales at 5,800 lb (2,631 kg), leaving 1,900 lb (862 kg) of payload left over for carrying luggage, gear and cargo. The trailer debuted at this year's Hershey RV Show in September and is available now for an MSRP starting at US$90,870.  Source: Pleasure-Way  Sign up for our FREE daily New Atlas newsletter!

Edel McAllister Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after it began trading on the stock market. So what exactly does it do and why is it so important? On this episode, technology writer with The Briefing Liz Carolan explains the background to the world's biggest stock market float. "It's the largest IPO ever, overtaking Musk's SpaceX, which was the largest IPO for the last five months. It's also, I mean, it's a big payday for a lot of people," Liz says. Although the share price has dropped back after the initial public offering, it’s still made eye-watering sums of money for its seven founders who are now worth over $20bn each. Liz gives us the background to the makers of the Claude chatbot and why it has overtaken OpenAI, the company that the Anthropic founders once worked at. "The main difference is that Anthropic has decided on a different business model really than ChatGPT. Their main kind of source of revenue, which has gone from zero in 2023 to $33bn in the first eight or nine months of this year, most of that is coming from corporate customers." Liz says Anthropic carved out a niche as suppliers of AI products to massive firms. "And then they're able to charge them subscriptions, but they're also able to charge them based on usage. And we're seeing that revenue really is the source of where the stuff is coming in." Is Grand Theft Auto 6 worth the wait?  Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history. We talk to gamer and content creator Shauna Davitt about whether it is worth the 13-year wait. The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the biggest and most popular games in history. Shauna says the controversial game is vast compared to GTA5. "The map is absolutely huge. I literally only have one tiny sliver of the map unlocked." The game also introduces a female lead character, Lucia, who joins boyfriend Jason on a crime spree. "It follows Jason and Lucia, basically on how they're surviving together and they get pulled into a job,’" Shauna explains, adding that while a part of it is about committing crime, the couple also do mundane things like DIY. Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than 24.5 million units, making about $2.36bn for the company. Shauna says this will increase when it goes interactive and people start buying in-game products. "When online drops next year, they'll make even more money with the amount of people going online to play with their friends." By Victor Tangermann    					Published				  					Nov 20, 2026 1:29 PM EST				  Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech For years now, analysts have warned of an AI bubble, which could pull the rug out from beneath the global economy if it were to pop. Despite their gloomy forecasts, a tech-saturated stock market rallied this summer, with the stock of core players like chipmaker Nvidia soaring to all-time highs. But after several weeks of bad news, baffling revelations — and the first-ever AI exclusive IPO, to top it all off — the stock market is now in free fall. By Friday afternoon, the Nasdaq Composite had wiped out all gains it made this year so far, a symbolic threshold indicating something is seriously amiss. Anthropic’s IPO, which sent shares soaring for a brief moment after it was publicly listed on Thursday, has plummeted from a record high of over $111 back down to just a hair above its original IPO listing of $83, a staggering 12 percent drop today alone. Its performance so far already puts it at odds with other AI-related IPOs, including SpaceX and Alibaba, which experienced less extreme drops.  Meanwhile, investors are piling their funds into Walmart, suggesting a rapidly changing tactic. It remains to be seen whether today’s major selloff is indicative of a larger downturn. But considering the S&P 500 has racked up losses on a daily basis for the last seven days of trading — the longest losing streak since 2020, per the Wall Street Journal — the consequences could be significant. The timing of the major sell-off, which comes in the immediate wake of Anthropic’s IPO, is particularly telling. It suggests investors are growing wary of the AI industry’s massive spending and debt accumulation. Companies have yet to provide evidence of a path of profitability as their costs continue to soar. “The AI buildout still needs vast amounts of funding just as financing costs are rising and signs of credit stress are emerging,” Swissquote senior analyst Ipek Ozkardeskaya told the WSJ. Investors are also wary of the federal government putting its foot down when it comes to policing the export of AI chips to China. The topic sits at the core of the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his extramarital affairs. Stronger export rules could significantly hurt the chipmaker’s bottom line, with estimates suggesting that as much as 20 percent of its revenue came from demand linked to China. It’s a precarious moment as Nivida finds itself without a permanent leader, the shares of the first AI company to go public are tanking, and the Dow is on track for a correction.  In short, there’s cause for concern — but it’s still too early to tell if the AI bubble is popping as we speak. Ahead of Thursday's (Nov 19) trading, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June. That's still over 17 per cent higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion. Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S&P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018. That would surpass the roughly 150 million km between Earth and the sun. The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million. There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau.
