Stellantis is about to throw in the towel on just about every single one of its motorsports endeavors other than NASCAR... which it just re-entered after a 14-year hiatus. On November 23, it's expected that the automaker will convene two extraordinary works council meetings with the ultimate outcome being a withdrawal. That means Peugeot would leave endurance racing (which admittedly hasn't been going too well), Citroën and Opel would drop out of Formula E, and Lancia's reborn rally team would bite the dust. The moves come as the automaker cuts costs across the board at the behest of CEO Antonio Filosa, according to Reuters. He's doing what he can to turn the company around after years of falling sales and weakening profitability. Earlier this year, Filosa launched a broad efficiency drive, known as the "Value Creation Program," and it targets about $6.6 billion in cost savings by 2028. Autocar reports that Stellantis Motorsport costs about $330 million a year to run, and cutting it could help with Stellantis' finances in Europe, where it just lost $341 million in the third quarter alone. This isn't the first time something like this has happened for Peugeot. Its former owners, PSA, quit the 24 Hours of Le Mans back in 2012 in an effort to save cash, and it didn't rejoin until 2022. It is, nevertheless, still strange timing. As I mentioned, Dodge just re-entered NASCAR. On top of that, French outlet L'Automobile reports that Peugeot has a redesigned 9x8 for its 2027 WEC endurance program and Citroën and Opel have been working on their new Gen4 car for Formula E with new technical partners. It's likely that the team that runs Citroën, MSG Racing, will continue with a new sponsor. Hell, Open is technically making its debut in FE this upcoming season. It was just announced in March of this year when the brand signed a four-year contract to compete with the new Gen4 cars. Lancia's WRC re-entry is another sacrificial lamb at the altar of financial prudence. The Lancia Corse HF team started in the WRC2 category this year, Autocar reports. It entered its gas-powered Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale, and it has even racked up a few wins. More likely than not, customer teams will continue to be supported, though. Motorsports are usually what's first to get cut when an automaker is struggling. Earlier this year, Alpine dropped out of WEC, citing a tough market, and Porsche did the same thing back in 2025.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition? Growth doesn’t always come from big strategies. Here are the small habits that had a bigger impact on my business than I ever expected.   		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a new service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook. Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business. None of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most. One of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly big difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine. The more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it. And it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target. Over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk. Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions. Walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses. And it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference. Now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself. Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business. Taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing new ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch. I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in new ones. Over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep. Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find new projects. One small habit that has made a big difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them. I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices. I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time. Over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%. I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more important today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching users’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers. Business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend. One habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage. I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return. Even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships. I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting. These relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals important or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch. Business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published. If you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.  Taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel important in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build. When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a new service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook. Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business. None of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most. Watch CBS News  Updated on:  November 20, 2026 / 9:25 PM EST             / CBS News            Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.  The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.  Both the  S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic. Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.  "The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over." The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email. "It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak. Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO. Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%. President Trump on Friday threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on U.S. tech companies if they build data centers in other countries.  "We're gonna fight very hard for the data centers," he said at a press conference Friday morning. "We're not gonna allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country." The president did not provide any specifics on how the tax plan might work and told reporters that he hadn't even informed members of his own administration of his intention to implement it.  Trump has been a persistent advocate of data center construction throughout his second term, calling the facilities a "Golden Goose" for the U.S. economy. That stance puts him at odds with the views of most Americans. Recent polls show that a strong majority of those surveyed oppose a new data center being built in their communities, while only a small percentage strongly support the idea. Even Republican voters are largely against data centers.   A few years ago, the typical American hardly ever thought about data centers. But they've become a major political issue seemingly overnight. We've seen local lawmakers lose their jobs over their support for new data center projects. Debates over the facilities were also a key pivot point in the midterm elections earlier this month, with exit polls showing that strong majorities of voters opposed having one built in their communities.   Lawmakers from both parties have responded to the dramatic shift against data centers by ramping up efforts to slow down, or even block entirely, data center construction. In July, New York became the first state to ban new data center projects. Similar proposals have been put forward in more than a dozen other states.  There has also been momentum in Congress behind plans to rein in data centers nationwide. One of those proposals, the Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA), passed through the House in a near-unanimous vote in September, but has been stalled in the Senate ever since.  The RPA would compel state utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard under which large data centers would cover the extra costs of upgrades. Several senators have pushed for separate legislation that represents much more aggressive efforts to curb data center-related utility costs. That includes a proposed bill that would empower federal regulators to force tech companies to cover certain costs that come from connecting their data centers to the grid.  A separate bipartisan bill, the GRID Act, would go even further by requiring all new data centers to have their own independent power supply that's completely separate from the public grid. Progressive lawmakers Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have called for a full, nationwide moratorium on new data centers "until strong national safeguards are in place."  All this is happening at a time when the president and the country's biggest tech companies are saying that the U.S. needs to dramatically increase its data capacity in order to build the economy of the future.  With that in mind, here are answers to some of the most important questions you may have about data centers, including why we need them, why thousands more are being built and what it means for local communities when a new data center comes to town.   Data centers are often called the "physical infrastructure of the internet." They are facilities where the servers, networking equipment and storage systems that allow digital data to be processed, stored and transmitted are housed.  At a fundamental level, the modern internet simply cannot exist without them. Every email, social media post, video or news article that you can find online runs through a data center.  There are an estimated 3,000 data centers currently operating across the United States, according to a Pew analysis of industry data published in April. The facilities aren't evenly distributed, though. Virginia has nearly 400, while data centers in some states number in the single digits.  There are roughly 1,500 new data centers in "various stages of development" nationwide, according to Pew. Other estimates suggest there could be as many as 3,000. But that doesn't just mean more of the same types of facilities that already exist are being built. Some of the proposed data centers are much larger than anything that's currently in operation. According to the power market tracking company Clearview, the biggest active data center in the U.S. has a power capacity of 750 megawatts. A single data center that's been proposed in Utah would have an estimated capacity of nearly 9,000 megawatts.  Data centers aren't just getting bigger. They're also being built in new places. Right now, the vast majority of active data centers are in urban areas, according to Pew. More than two-thirds of the incoming data centers will be in rural areas.  The more we ask the internet to do, the more computing power is needed to meet our demands.  Over the course of the past two decades, the U.S. has had to steadily build more and more data centers as so many aspects of our lives have moved online. But the recent, dramatic increase in data center projects isn't being driven by the spread of social media, the rise of streaming or the remote work revolution. It's being driven by AI. AI works by processing huge data sets to learn, adapt and make predictions in a way that typical algorithms can't. That takes a lot of processing power. The kind of processing power that America's data infrastructure simply won't be able to handle as AI becomes more complex and widespread, without a massive increase in data center capacity.  Tech companies are pouring money into building more data centers to support their lofty AI ambitions, which many see as a world-changing technology that will be at the core of everything we do. One estimate found that it could take $6.7 trillion in global data center investment before the end of the decade to create the scale of computing power that's needed to support AI's continued growth.  Data centers have been around in some form as long as computers have. Until recently, most Americans had no real strong opinion about them, if they were aware of their existence at all. But public opinion has shifted dramatically against data centers over a remarkably short period of time, as people across the country are being faced with the prospect of having one built in their back communities.  The share of Americans who say they would strongly oppose a new data center near where they live more than doubled, growing from 24% to 55%, in the span of just nine months, according to a June poll by Heatmap. Other surveys have shown that a strong majority of Americans do not want data centers built in their communities.  Anti-data center sentiment has been especially intense in areas where they're being built. There's a growing list of local lawmakers who have been voted out after approving the construction of new facilities. A recent study tracked the creation of hundreds of new local Facebook groups with more than 400,000 total members dedicated to bringing residents together in opposition to proposed data centers in their communities. There are many reasons people cite for why they oppose data centers. The most prominent concerns center around the amount of resources the facilities consume. Data centers use up a ton of electricity and need a lot of water to keep all those servers from overheating.  New facilities are also massive construction projects, which bring all sorts of disruptions to communities while they're being built — road closures, construction noise, huge trucks clogging up streets and more.  Many data center critics say it's just unpleasant to live near one. One of the main complaints is noise, which some residents have described as like having a "freight train" constantly running past their homes. Researchers have found that large data centers can have a "heat island" effect that makes the surrounding area noticeably hotter.  Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest against AI data center expansion in Imperial, California on July 18, 2026. Broader skepticism of AI is also a big factor. Tech companies have argued that the U.S. needs to build all of these new data centers to support their vision of an AI-powered future. But more Americans say they expect AI to have a negative impact on society when you account for how it will affect the labor market, education, environment and our personal relationships. It's a tough sell to ask people to tolerate the downsides of having a data center in their community when they don't want the products that the facilities are being built to support. Finally, there's the phenomenon commonly known as NIMBYism. The acronym, which stands for Not In My Back Yard, is often used derisively to describe people who say they support the construction of things our society needs — affordable housing, power plants, prisons and public transportation — but refuse to accept those things being built where they live. In the eyes of some proponents of data centers, local opposition to building them is a classic case of NIMBYism in action.  A lot. In 2024, data centers accounted for 4% of all power consumption in the United States. With so many facilities being built, the total amount of electricity data centers consume is projected to more than double by 2030, according to estimates from the International Energy Agency. A separate study estimated that data centers could account for up to 12% of all power usage in the U.S. by 2028.  A typical newly built "hyperscale" facility can require as much power as 100,000 households. The largest data centers can consume more energy than entire major cities, and demand is higher in places with the most facilities. In Virginia, for example, data centers consumed 40% of the state's electricity in 2024, according to a Bloomberg analysis.  Utility companies have also spent billions building out transmission lines and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the local power grid and building new power plants to meet increased demand.  It's important to note that all of the tangible information we have on data centers and energy prices is based on what's already been built. At this point, experts can only estimate what will happen when all of those new proposed facilities eventually begin operating.  That said, there's already evidence that the data centers that are currently online have had an impact on electricity rates, thanks to a combination of higher operational costs for utilities and increased demand.  Residential power rates have roughly doubled over the past 10 years. How much data centers are to blame for that increase is the source of significant debate. Some recent analyses have found that states with the most data centers have seen their energy rates climb at a faster rate than the national average. But another study suggested that their impact on electricity bills has been modest — at least so far. Some in the energy and tech industries even argue that data centers can actually lower energy prices. While there's some evidence to support that claim in certain areas, most experts believe the large-scale buildout of data centers across the country will push prices higher in the long run.  A variety of solutions have been proposed to keep that from happening, including forcing data center companies to pay for any new infrastructure or plants that utilities have to build to power them, charging the centers higher rates than typical consumers and even requiring data centers to have their own on-site power plants.   An aerial view of the Stargate Oracle AI data center campus in Abilene, Texas. Data centers use water to keep the thousands of servers and other equipment they house from overheating. One estimate found that the typical non-hyperscale data center uses about 300,000 gallons of water per day, about as much as 1,000 U.S. households. Newer, larger facilities can use as much as 5 million gallons every day.  In total, data centers used up an estimated 66 billion gallons of water in 2023, according to an analysis by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That same study estimated that data center water demand could double by 2028. While that is a lot of water, it's a relatively small share of the 117 trillion gallons the United States uses every year, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.  There are also ways to significantly reduce the amount of water data centers use. Historically, most data centers relied on what's known as an open-loop cooling system, in which water is brought in, then evaporated to cool the air around servers. While that's the cheapest way to prevent servers from overheating, it's also very inefficient. There are other, closed-loop approaches that allow facilities to reuse water, which can cut a data center's water demand by up to 70%. More than half of all global data centers still rely on open-loop systems, but some of the biggest companies in the tech industry, including OpenAI, have said they plan to prioritize closed-loop facilities moving forward.   That change only addresses the water that data centers use directly. The facilities also impact water supplies in a larger way through their electricity consumption. The vast majority of power plants in the U.S. use water to keep their own systems from overheating. As a result, the extra strain that data centers put on electricity providers accounts for an additional 800 billion gallons of water consumed annually, according to Lawrence Berkeley Lab.  OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has tried to appease concerns about water usage, telling the Sources Podcast in September that data centers use no more water than an office building and that 38,000 ChatGPT queries use as much water as the production of one almond. It's a claim that many experts feel is difficult to verify given the limited amount of public information made available by AI companies and the number of vairables at play when trying to acuurately analyze each data center's water usage. Like any major construction project, a new data center creates a lot of short-term jobs while it's being built. But once it's completed and operational, the facilities take a relatively small number of people to keep them running. The average data center creates between 100 and 200 permanent full-time jobs locally, according to a recent study by the Brookings Institution.  Of course, data centers don't only affect employment at the local level. The entire U.S. economy relies on the existence of infrastructure that allows us to consistently and reliably send information over the internet. At a very basic level, we need data centers. The questions of how many we need, where they should go and who should bear the costs are where the real debate lies.  AI Audio Computing Gaming Home Entertainment Phones Puzzle hints Science Streaming VPN Wearables Deals Advertise (opens in new tab) About our ads (opens in new tab) Licensing (opens in new tab) Careers (opens in new tab) Help (opens in new tab) Feedback (opens in new tab) Sitemap (opens in new tab) © 2026 Yahoo. GTA 6 sales might be booming, but actual brick-and-mortar stores aren't benefiting from Rockstar's good fortune  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Grand Theft Auto 6 is already shattering records after a 13-year wait, generating with its 99 on Metacritic and more than 24 million units in pre-sales alone before officially dropping on Thursday. Yet for brick-and-mortar video game stores, the biggest entertainment launch in history is leaving them out of the party and clanging the death knell for physical media. RELATED: GTA 6 Review "A cover-to-cover masterpiece without equal." Because Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two Interactive opted to release GTA 6 strictly as a digital download, leaving physical retail cases with nothing inside but a paper download code, local shops are failing to benefit from the boom GTA 6 has given to the industry.      Speaking to the BBC over here in the UK, Richard Tewksbury, owner of the independent UK shop Super Game Shack in Leicester, called his store's GTA 6 numbers "embarrassing." Despite calling the game itself "amazing," Tewksbury revealed he had sold just five copies in total: four on PlayStation 5 and one on Xbox. "It's because it's all digital. No one sadly wants to buy a code in a box," Tewksbury said. "We gave it a little go, but they just knocked it dead with making it digital. For game shops, it's a write-off." The humongous file size of GTA 6 hasn’t helped either, with players encouraged to pre-load days in advance from home. Tewksbury noted that most gamers aren't even thinking about local stores anymore, a grim preview of what's coming after Sony announced in July that it will end physical PlayStation disc production entirely by January 2028. Rob Spence, a Physical media collector interviewed by the BBC, echoed that frustration. Warning that the shift toward digital-only releases threatens both independent storefronts and the social concept of gaming. Beyond losing the ability to hold the artwork or build a shelf collection "that can't ever be taken away from you," Spence lamented the death of midnight launch parties and Saturday-morning store runs. The exact kind of "community feel" and "sense of belonging" that once defined major game launches.      The same exact situation is playing out on a massive scale across the US, where the largest standalone video game retailer is publicly pushing back against publishers abandoning discs. On the eve of GTA 6’s launch, GameStop Corp. CEO Ryan Cohen criticized the industry's digital pivot, calling it a mistake that hurts both retailers and everyday players. Speaking to Bloomberg, Cohen argued that replacing discs with $80 digital downloads, and hollow "code in a box" retail cases, strips gamers of basic ownership rights. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen said. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop." For decades, GameStop’s business has relied heavily on pre-owned trade-ins, giving players a cheaper way to play major releases (as well as the option to trade the disc in again when they are done). Without discs in circulation, that market is rapidly dying.  Pre-owned and refurbished products made up 22% of GameStop’s sales (roughly $171 million) in the quarter ending August 1, marking a sharp 32% drop from the year prior. According to Cohen, publishers are eager to kill off the secondhand market because "removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying new." Even for a Goliath in the industry like GTA 6, the midnight-line hype of days gone by simply hasn’t been a thing at US stores.      As physical discs edge closer to extinction, accelerated by disc-less console options and Sony’s 2028 cutoff, gamers on both sides of the Atlantic have grown increasingly vocal about digital storefronts delisting games or shutting down servers, rendering paid titles unplayable. Now Microsoft have of course, tried to soften the blow for existing collectors with its Disc-to-Digital program, which lets players insert eligible Xbox One and Xbox Series discs to unlock transferable digital licenses across their accounts. But while it’s a genuinely consumer-friendly system for game preservation, it ultimately serves as a bridge for older libraries rather than any kind of meaningful lifeline for the used-disc industry. Especially when massive new releases like GTA 6 don’t print a disc to begin with.      While PlayStation has made its intentions of an all-digital future clear, Microsoft has stayed noticeably mute on whether Xbox Helix will include a disc drive. Recently, a Microsoft job listing did advertise an "Xbox Games Supply Strategist." According to the posting, the role is tasked with coordinating "the launch of physical Xbox games across all platforms.” Whether that means Xbox Helix will ship with a traditional optical disc drive, we really don’t know yet. But as PlayStation draws a hard line against physical games, Microsoft has a golden opportunity to score major goodwill with collectors and brick-and-mortar shoppers if it keeps physical media alive on Helix. Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.  The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C. And, yeah, they live up to the hype. While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music. The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes. The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.  As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable. For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.  Sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that. Would you try these? Major League Baseball players have rejected management's proposal for an international amateur draft Major League Baseball players rejected management's proposal for an international amateur draft, instead asking Friday for larger signing bonus pools under the current system and more rewards for small-market teams in another sign the sport is heading to a lockout next month. Management has tried unsuccessfully for more than two decades to get an international draft and in June proposed it start with 12 rounds in 2027. “We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with new artificial restrictions like a draft,” players' association head Bruce Meyer said in a statement after a bargaining session in New York. MLB's five-year collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. EST on Dec. 1 and management is expected to immediately lock out players in the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972. Owners are pushing for a salary cap, which players say they never will agree to, sparking a confrontation that threatens the 2027 season. An amateur draft was established for residents of the U.S. and Canada in 1965 and extended to residents of U.S. territories such as Puerto Rico in 1990. A signing bonus pool system started in 2012 restrained team spending for amateurs residing outside those areas, primarily teenagers from the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Colombia, Mexico and Panama. Players outside the U.S. are eligible to sign as young as 16, and it's common for players, their families and trainers to strike handshake deals with teams at 13 or 14 in a system rife with corruption. “We continue to believe it is long past time to reform the system in ways that would address longstanding challenges and benefit future players,” MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said. "The enhanced transparency of the international draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system.”  Caplin also said MLB dropped its proposal that would have made high school players ineligible for the domestic amateur draft, citing “feedback we received from the MLBPA.” The union proposed teams entering into any agreements with international amateurs ahead of a signing period lose the right to sign the involved player, forfeit pool space in the amount of the agreed-upon signing bonus and their entire pool space in the subsequent signing period. The lost pool space would be redistributed to other clubs and a violation would result in a minimum $200,000 fine. In addition, the sides would hire a joint compliance officer. MLB has tried to gain an international draft since 2001 only to be repeatedlyrebuffed by players.  In its latest proposal, management included $200 million in signing bonus pools for 2027, roughly equal to 2026 international amateur spending, and said it would retain an unlimited amount of passed over players signing for up to $10,000 each. Management proposed hard slots for each draft pick and asked the minimum signing age for international amateurs to be raised to 18 from 17 on the Sept. 1 of their signing year. Players proposed increases in the three basic team pool levels in 2027: from $8,034,900 to $8.5 million, from $7,357,100 to $7.75 million and from $6,679,200 to $7 million. The figures would grow in future years at the same rate as industry revenue. Teams would be allowed to exceed their bonus pools but would be taxed on their overage and if 15% or more over could lose future pool amounts. Additional pool space of up to $2 million would be added to club rewards in the Prospect Promotion Incentive begun under the current CBA. The union asked that the limit of bonuses not counting against the pools be raised to $75,000 through 2029 and then $100,000, and that the limit of 60% additional pool allotment a team can acquire be dropped along with the requirement traded allotments be in $250,000 increments. Players signing below $75,000 would be eligible for $25,000 promotion bonuses if assigned to a complex team or a player development league club, money to be funded centrally by MLB. In addition, the union proposed that teams receiving revenue sharing money be able to increase their pool by $1 million in a single signing period over a five-year agreement and by $500,000 in each period following a postseason appearance. Those teams also would be able to sign two draft-eligible players to a major league contract from 2027-31 but would lose $4 million per player in allotment.  Players asked to set up separate signing bonus pools for eligible players with limited foreign professional experience, preventing future players in that situation from competing for signing bonus pool money with teenage prospects — as Roki Sasaki did when he signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers before the 2025 season. “Our proposals help build upon baseball’s advances as an international game, while safeguarding the interests of young athletes who are the future of our sport,” Meyer said. ___ See AP’s full MLB coverage here 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

The last post was about the development toolbar Muru adds to each HTML page under muructl run, with the record Muru keeps of each request. That record can say a lot about how a request was served, how long it waited for a worker, how long the application took, what it logged and what went wrong. What it can't say is what the application did with its time, because Muru only sees the application from the outside. For that, Muru uses wrapture, the package I wrote for monkey patching, testing and tracing, which I covered in a series of posts earlier this year. With tracing turned on, wrapture's instrumentation records the calls the application makes while it serves a request, such as its database queries and calls to other services, and the toolbar gains panels showing them. The shop from the last post is a Flask application which uses sqlite3 for its database, and urllib.request to call its stock service. Tracing needs wrapture and its instrumentation packages added to the project: then tracing = true, and a wrapture configuration saying what to instrument, which can go in the same pyproject.toml: The flask instrumentation records each request with the view that handled it, sqlite3 records each query, with statement = true so the SQL itself is kept, and urllib.request records calls made with it. The configuration can also be in a wrapture.toml file beside pyproject.toml, or a file named by WRAPTURE_CONFIG, which is where wrapture itself would look for it. I have also put toolbar = true in the [tool.muru.run] table this time, so the toolbar is on without needing --toolbar each time. When the run starts, the host says where the configuration came from and what it instruments: Not everyone working on a project may want tracing on, since it adds work to every request. tracing = true in the muru.local.toml beside the project turns it on for my own runs only, with the configuration still coming from the project. Tracing needs Python 3.12 or later, and if wrapture is missing, or its configuration can't be found or applied, the run logs a one-line warning saying why and serves the application untraced, rather than failing to start. With tracing on, the front page's badge now shows two hints, and the toolbar opens on them:  The toolbar also has new tabs, Trace, SQL and Outbound. The Trace panel is the request's tree of operations, on the same clock as the Timing panel from the last post:  The view ran one query for the books, and then for each book, a query for its author and a call to the stock service. This is the code which did that: Nothing about it looks wrong when reading it, and with eight books, the whole page took under ten milliseconds. It is a different story with a thousand books, a database on another machine, and a stock service on the other side of a network. The Trace panel shows the pattern when there are only a few books, but with hundreds it would be a very long list. The SQL panel groups the request's queries by statement, with how many times each ran and their total time, and then lists each query in order:  Statements which differ only in the values written into them group together, so the author query shows up as one statement run eight times. This is the N+1 pattern, one query for the list and then one more for each row of it, and it is one of the most common performance problems in web applications which use a database. It is also easy to write without noticing, since an ORM will happily generate it from code that looks perfectly reasonable. The Outbound panel does the same for calls to other services, grouped by method, host and path:  A path segment which names a row rather than the endpoint, such as a number, a UUID or a long hexadecimal string, is grouped as {id}, so the eight calls to /stock/1 through /stock/8 are one endpoint called eight times. Calls made with requests, httpx, urllib3, aiohttp and http.client are recorded the same way, given the instrumentation for them, as are gRPC calls. The fix for both is to ask for everything at once. A join gets the authors with the books, and the stock service can answer for several books in one call: Saving the file was enough for the run to start a new release with the change: and the front page's record now has one query and one call: The two hints went with them. Hints are where I would start with any page, since they apply the same thresholds to every request without me having to remember what to look for. A statement run five or more times in one request, or an endpoint called five or more times, is flagged, as is a single query or call taking a quarter or more of the request's time and at least 10 milliseconds. The author page from the last post still divides by zero for an author with no books. With tracing on, its Trace panel shows where the exception went:  The view, author, is marked as failed, since the exception escaped it. The request is marked as well, because Flask's instrumentation notes the exception Flask's error handling caught against the request. The Exceptions panel lists both, the one Flask handled being marked as such: The bars also show something the Errors panel didn't. The view itself was done in about a third of a millisecond, out of a request which took about three. Most of the rest went on Flask handling the exception, which includes formatting and logging the traceback. The shop gets its request spans from the flask instrumentation, and there is the same for Django and other frameworks. An application without such instrumentation, such as a plain WSGI or ASGI callable, can have Muru wrap its entry point in wrapture's request middleware instead: The same key in a mount's table wraps just that mount, for an application which mixes WSGI and ASGI. It shouldn't be used where a framework's instrumentation already records requests, since the middleware would then record them instead, and the framework's own request settings would no longer apply. How tracing is set up follows from how Muru starts an application, as covered in the import once, fork many post. The host process applies the wrapture configuration before it imports the application, so the instrumentation's patches are in place for the application's own imports. What the configuration sends events to, its sinks, are only started in each worker after it is forked, so the host holds no threads or open files of wrapture's when it forks. The toolbar's panels don't need a sink at all, since Muru collects what wrapture records for each request itself. Any sinks the configuration does declare still work as they would without Muru. Adding wrapture's printer sink, for example, prints each request's tree in the run's output, from the worker which served it: Each worker writes its own output, so a sink writing to a file needs {pid} in its path to give each worker a file of its own. The same is true under muructl serve and the Muru daemon, except there is no toolbar there, so tracing costs only what the configuration's own sinks do. In production that would normally mean exporting to an OpenTelemetry collector, as covered in the OpenTelemetry export in wrapture post. Between them, the toolbar and tracing answer most of what I want to know about a request while I'm working on an application. How long it waited and why, what it logged and what failed, and what the application did with its time, all without adding anything to the application beyond a dependency and a few lines of configuration. The toolbar's Timing panel has one more row, for modules a request loads for the first time in its worker, and that is where the next post, when lazy imports help, picks up. Lazy imports are popular for making command line tools start faster, but in a web server which imports an application once and forks its workers, deferring an import is a trade, and Muru has the measurements to make it. BlackRock’s IBIT posted its largest daily outflow on record, taking three-session outflows near $900 million as BTC dipped amid a broader market selloff. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $582 million in net outflows on Thursday, led by a record withdrawal from BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT). IBIT posted $541 million in outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day withdrawal since launching in January 2024, according to Farside Investors data. The figure surpassed its previous daily record of $528.3 million, set on Jan. 30, 2026. IBIT shares closed Thursday at $35.08, down 0.8% for the session. The shares have fallen 24.2% over the past month and 29.4% year to date, according to Yahoo Finance. Thursday marked IBIT’s third consecutive trading day of outflows, totaling nearly $900 million. The latest streak followed a single day of inflows on Monday, which ended 11 straight sessions of withdrawals totaling roughly $2.35 billion. The selling brought US spot Bitcoin ETFs’ November outflows to $3.47 billion, pushing their 2026 net withdrawals to approximately $3.11 billion, according to SoSoValue data. Bitcoin (BTC) traded at around $61,875 at publishing time, down 3% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. The crypto asset was down 9.8% over the past seven days. The ETF withdrawals coincided with a broader market selloff Thursday, as Anthropic’s highly anticipated stock market debut failed to sustain gains in AI-related stocks, including Nvidia, amid concerns over high valuations and heavy spending on artificial intelligence. In the spring of last year, a striking collection of individuals gathered for a lavish, expensive dinner event at the Trump National Golf Club Washington, D.C., in honor of President Donald Trump’s newly debuted $TRUMP memecoin–a thing that any functioning democratic society would of course never allow to be connected directly to the chief executive of the country. The assembled group was a motley crew–cryptocurrency “enthusiasts” and evangelists, political toadies, foreign businessmen looking for access to the President, etc. The one thing they shared in common was disposable income: In order to attend the event, which was open to the top 185 holders of the $TRUMP memecoin, you needed to possess more than $55,000 in $TRUMP. That was the cheapest ticket for anyone who attended. Most attendees had “invested” far more, into the hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars range. The presumed objective for anyone present was to boost their standing in the eyes of the White House, for the sake of favorable treatment … and there were probably a sprinkling of utter fools in there who also thought they would actually be making money on $TRUMP. Now two years into Trump’s second term, even the dumbest would-be crypto zealot in Trump’s orbit has no doubt been disabused of the notion that the existence of the memecoin (and all the others like it) had any other function than to line the Trump family’s pockets. Since its high-water market at the beginning of 2025, when it reached an all-time high of $73.43, $TRUMP has now lost about 99% of its value, recently breaching even the sub-$1 mark. There is essentially no “investor” in it who hasn’t lost everything they put into the coin. And although it’s not hard to find a delusional fan of the POTUS out there who loses tens of thousands of dollars on a scam and then inexplicably blames the Democrats for it, the blame has quite clearly also fallen on Trump, even if people are loath to actively voice it. Look no further than the 2026 version of Trump’s crypto dinner happening this weekend, when you can get in the doors and be one of the “top 185” holders of the memecoin just by dropping … around $500 in investment. From $55,000 to $500, in just over a year! 📉 “Interest in Trump’s meme coin dinner fades as $TRUMP sinks to record lows” Michelle Conlin, Tom Bergin for @reuters.com [image or embed] — Zach Everson (@zacheverson.com) 10:51 AM · Nov 16, 2026  What this tells us is that the actual demand to attend said dinner featuring not only Donald Trump, but luminaries like boxer Floyd Mayweather and Shark Tank dingus Kevin O’Leary (who both have plenty of shady crypto entanglements) has pretty much entirely dried up. The Washington Post reported that a buyer by the name of “Michel” was able to reach No. 179 on the leaderboard of $TRUMP holders immediately before the scoring period ended by spending just $518–hilariously, the actual value of those $TRUMP holdings has apparently been cut in half even since that purchase was recently made. The Post likewise found that when they compared the leaderboard of $TRUMP holders with the registered attendees of the dinner, there were more than 5,000 people who could have qualified to attend this weekend’s dinner simply by filling out a form to accept their invite. None of them did. The dinner’s organizers, meanwhile, also extended signups by four days past the original deadline. Sounds like things are going well? So who is actually going to be in attendance, then? Well, foreign nationals and businessmen for one, according to a CBS investigation. They found that of the 130 crypto wallets shown at the top of the leaderboard calculating eligibility for the dinner, 79 of the those 130 had their $TRUMP coin on exchanges unavailable to American consumers, with wallets holding roughly $8.8 million in $TRUMP. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said of those optics, “Foreign nationals and bad actors are apparently only too happy to seek access and favors by buying into Trump’s meme coin scheme,” in a statement to the network. Trump getting big crypto bribes from China again. www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-c… [image or embed] — emptywheel (@emptywheel.bsky.social) 9:30 AM · Nov 18, 2026  The crypto industry is of course not going down without a fight in its efforts to avoid meaningful regulation, and it continued to spend hundreds of millions of dollars in the just-concluded midterm election cycle boosting the candidates it views as friendly to cryptocurrency. But the overall crypto market remains mired in a long winter, and the blue wave midterm elections did little to assuage the fears of speculative investors who for so long claimed that Bitcoin and its descendants would completely reshape global commerce and banking. If that kind of rhetoric sounds familiar to you, it would no doubt be because the same overheated language is now mostly reserved for artificial intelligence, which is where the speculative dollars now mostly end up. Bitcoin, always the largest and most resilient cryptocurrency, has continued to slide at least modestly in the time since the midterms concluded, with expectations of rising interest rates and a massive hack of the Binance exchange not helping matters. In Congress, the crypto industry’s heavily lobbied Digital Market Clarity Act has also been frozen in the Senate, now likely in need of a total rework in the face of an incoming Democratic majority. Amid these doldrums for the industry, Trump has of course remained a major crypto booster, and why wouldn’t he be? Creators of memecoins like Trump (and even Hunter Biden!) found the perfect dodge; an ability to make gobs of money through things like licensing fees even as the coin they launch loses all its value and leaves “investors” completely wiped out. It’s worked out great for them–as reported in a Reuters investigation not long ago, the Trump family and companies have earned at least $2.3 billion from four separate crypto ventures as of this spring, while they simultaneously estimated that outside investors in five Trump-linked crypto ventures have lost more than $5 billion. These monetary losers managed to find the ultimate way to funnel money in the general direction of the presidency while avoiding legal pitfalls. You have to wonder what the vibes truly will be like at this weekend’s dinner in Virginia, as the guests who lost 99% of their investment in a memecoin in the last year are entertained by the no-doubt captivating performance of mentalist Lior Suchard. Can you imagine what a group of legitimate investors would say to the guest of honor and coin namesake when he arrived, after losing them this kind of money? Somehow, I don’t get the sense that Donald Trump will be received by them in quite the same way. It’s almost as if “investing” was never truly the point. Like what you just read? Retail investors traded $772 million in Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most Vanda Research has recorded for a market debut since 2012. Retail investors traded $772 million in Anthropic shares on its Nasdaq debut Thursday, but their net purchases totaled just $60 million, about half the $118 million they put into SpaceX on its first day of trading in June. Anthropic’s first-day retail trading volume topped SpaceX’s $669 million and was the highest for any market debut in Vanda Research’s data, which go back to 2012, Yahoo Finance reported. Volume counts both purchases and sales, while net buying measures how much purchases exceeded sales. The Claude AI developer and its existing shareholders offered 980 million shares at $83 each in the $81.34 billion initial public offering (IPO). Anthropic shares opened on Nasdaq at $111.50 on Thursday, 34.3% above the IPO price, and closed at $97.17 for a first-day gain of 17.1%. SpaceX shares gained 19.2% in their June 12 debut, closing at $160.95 against an IPO price of $135, according to Nasdaq. Although Anthropic’s base offering exceeded SpaceX’s initial $75 billion sale, SpaceX ultimately raised $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their option to purchase additional shares. Before the IPO, Vanda forecast about $250 million in net retail buying, more than four times Thursday’s total. Its forecast drew on retail trading in past market debuts and the volume of Anthropic perpetual futures traded on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Shortly before Nasdaq trading began, those futures traded at $110.48, just 0.9% below the stock’s opening price. Given that Jensen defenders have been depicting Jensen Huang as essential to Nvidia’s so-called circular financing, the “Bank of Nvidia” needs to be rebranded as the “Bank of Jensen.” A new Wall Street Journal story provides much more detail on a scheme we covered briefly in our earlier Nvidia coverage. Nvidia had solicited Wall Street heavyweights like Blackstone, KKR and Brookfield  to provide $500 billion in funding to Nvidia customers. An October Reuters report described how the program was not getting off the ground due to an unbridgeable gap between the level of financial support the money mavens wanted and what Nvidia provided. The new Journal story has a lot more insider-y detail than the October Reuters account did. While that makes for a more entertaining read, the focus on the gossip (admittedly, reporter finds) has the effect of obscuring the bigger story architecture. As we pointed out earlier, Nvidia was suffering a big drop in market share that had started in 2023,1 hence the eagerness to sell GPUs to Chinese buyers. The article describes how Jensen was concerned about the fall in Nvidia’s multiple and wanted to gin up more financing from outside parties to goose it back up. That is a tacit admission that he was seeking more leverage to create the appearance of better performance. Leverage both amplifies profits and losses.  It may also be that Jensen realized he was approaching the limits of what he could do with his circular financing gimmicks. Even very deep tech pockets like Amazon were open about increasingly needing to use debt to fund AI capex.2 It is hardly a secret that across the industry,  planned expenditures even once cash-rich tech giants exceed what they could fund out of their own cash flow and funds on hand, since AI is still a very long way from being a sensible economic proposition.  The Journal story also describes how Jensen was getting resistance for some of his financing ideas from then CFO, now interim CEO Colette Kriss. It would not be surprising if it emerged that some of Jensen’s transactions were not papered up properly (there have already been ample reports of him dong deals on a handshake) and that auditors may have started clearing their throats.  It is also surprising to sees a supposedly business-savvy media outlet seem shocked, shocked that a briefly noised-up funding scheme with Big Names attached to it did not materialize. Admittedly, this one got a bit more profile than some other too-clever ideas due to Jensen making lots of noise to goose Nvidia stock and perhaps also out of the naive belief that media amplification would pressure the money mavens to deliver. Recall that I repeatedly warned readers that the oft-mentioned Ukraine reconstruction fund, with fundraising led by BlackRock, was an obvious entry in hall of hollow mandates. The big tell was that BlackRock was merely an advisor and had committed no funds.  The short version of the breathless Wall Street Journal story is that Jensen Huang’s sense of manhood was offended in June when he learned that Apollo and Blackstone publicized in June that they were providing $35 billion of funding for Nvidia competitor Broadcom for chips for Anthropic. Nvidia and six  Wall Street titans announced $500 billion program in August. That has not gotten done. One of the reason stated is that Huang would not provide anywhere near as much in the way of guarantees  as Broadcom had. Aside from that being an issue in and of itsellf,  vastly bigger program would likely require even better terms.  From the Journal in Wall Street Pledged to Mobilize $500 Billion for Nvidia—but Hasn’t Put Up a Dime. You can see “pledged” is a stretch; the text even states “But the promise was short on substance.” This idea appears only to have gotten to the pitch outline stage, and was not even commemorated in a non-binding memorandum of understanding. Admittedly, the Journal’s earlier reporting in August indicated otherwise. First from that article, Nvidia, Wall Street Firms Strike AI Financing Deal Targeting $500 Billion: Nvidia reached deals with some of Wall Street’s largest firms aimed at raising massive amounts of capital to help the chip maker’s customers finance the cost of computing power. The chip maker has signed agreements to partner with Apollo Global Management, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, to establish “compute financing platforms,” the companies announced Monday. The firms aim to deploy over $500 billion of outside capital in the coming years. The firms said the platforms will create pools of capital at “attractive rates” for Nvidia customers.  “These financing platforms will help customers access scarce compute at scale and build the AI factories that will power every industry and country in the age of AI,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said. Apollo and Blackstone earlier this year struck a deal with Broadcom to set up a similar financing platform for the chip maker’s customers. The platform will offer financing to companies like Anthropic to pay for computing power from chips developed by Broadcom, including Google’s processing units. This all sounds extremely fuzzy. Importantly, the story does not identify any firm as the equivalent of a lead manager to herd the other cats.  The August article showed investors were not convinced: Nvidia’s stock ended Monday down nearly 3% after the Financial Times earlier reported the deal.  The underlying Financial Times story also said Nvidia said it had signed a memorandum of understanding.3 As we indicated in our earlier post, the skeptics were soon proven correct. It was in October that Reuters reported in  Nvidia’s bet that its chips can finance the AI boom gets a Wall Street reality check that this program was stuck on the runway. The money quote from that account: Nvidia’s plan, announced with financiers including Blackstone, Apollo and KKR in August, had envisioned using chips as ​collateral with limited guarantee in order to allow AI developers a way to facilitate their access to Nvidia’s compute. The strategy was seen as an expensive but necessary way to create a financing market similar to that used in the leasing of aircraft. Nvidia has said that some of the deals could have no ​more than a 25% residual value guarantee, saying the initiative is designed to address concerns around circular financing. This was seen as offering less support than other recent AI financing deals, raising expectations among some on Wall Street that Nvidia would need to get more creative Now to the Journal’s new piece: In August, he [Huang] got pledges from several firms—Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR—to mobilize an astounding sum: $500 billion. The announcement created the splash Huang wanted… The wave of money was supposed to help Nvidia’s startup customers—from OpenAI and Anthropic to smaller, weaker ones—finance the chips they needed to buy, keeping Nvidia’s sales humming well into the future. They were seeking to turn chip financing into a standardized asset class. Let’s stop here. This idea is ridiculous on its face. If Nvidia or Broadcom had been engaged in somewhat standard financing, they could easily have sold those loans to a private credit fund or a CLO. The fact that, as far as I can tell, that has or has not much happened says that either these borrowings would be viewed at too poor in quality (as in BBB or worse if rated) so as to be sold at the par value of the loan.  The alternative would be some sort of secured financing, as in selling payments made on GPUs or even GPUs themselves as collateral. But GPUs are too short-lived for that. Their value falls when newer, more powerful GPUs are released. Even though the Braodcom funding did get done, it required a very large residual value guarantee, one that Nvidia was not prepared to match. Such a large guarantee means from a credit perspective that the borrowing is not stand-alone, but both the end borrower and the guarantor’s creditworthiness need to be evaluate. Back to the Journal:  But the promise was short on substance. To date, no capital has actually been deployed, according to people familiar with the matter. And investors are increasingly skeptical that the program will reach its lofty ambitions now that Huang has been ousted over a sex and suspected spy scandal that has engulfed Nvidia. Nvidia had already begun to rein in the backstops and guarantees it uses to grease lending, partly under the skepticism of finance chief Colette Kress, who has now become the interim CEO. Those guarantees are crucial to Wall Street’s willingness to finance the chips, and Kress on Tuesday signaled to investors that the company will be disciplined in the deals it supports…. Frustrated that Nvidia’s valuation multiple was dropping at the start of the year despite jaw-dropping profit, Huang began to focus on levers he could pull, people familiar with his thinking said. Yet Huang seemed resistant to the premise that investors were increasingly punishing Nvidia for too much in the way of financial backstops to companies in its ecosphere. The Journal later notes: The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was considering providing a $250 billion backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio. The next day, Nvidia shares fell by 5%, wiping out $250 billion in market value. The market’s negative reaction prompted Nvidia to rework its deal and cut its initial financial commitment to OpenAI in half, the Journal reported. News Corp, owner of The Wall Street Journal, has a content-licensing partnership with OpenAI. So the big bright idea was that getting big Wall Street names involved would reassure equity investors:  Nvidia was concerned the market would think it was taking on too much risk and it wanted to signal that other investors were ready to help finance chips. The ballyhooed deal was a napkin doodle: The half-trillion-dollar memorandum of understanding the firms signed was just a few pages that specified a fundraising target, the profile of target customers and that Nvidia would consider providing credit backstops on a case-by-case basis, people familiar with the matter said. The investment firms involved aren’t committed to actually raising any money, and the $500 billion figure isn’t meaningful, the people said. The idea behind the agreement was to signal that financing will be available, and get major Wall Street partners thinking about how to solve a complex issue, the people said. Analysts applauded the company’s ability to move itself out of the center of financing its customers. But they were quick to note the aspirational nature of the firms’ agreement to work together on raising $500 billion “over time.”… Huang was not willing to give what had become market terms for this sort of scheme: Huang said in August that the credit support Nvidia was willing to provide would top out at 25% of the cost of a project. That is a lower level of backing than rivals agreed to. Broadcom provided a residual-value guarantee for about 85% of Project Big Sky, the $35 billion financing for Anthropic announced in June. For Project North Star, a $63 billion follow-up financing, Broadcom’s residual-value guarantee covered a little under three-quarters of the transaction. Credit markets have grown more skeptical of AI-linked borrowers with low credit ratings since early August, and investors have been pushing for a larger than 25% residual value guarantee to get comfortable with lending, people familiar with the matter said, a potential roadblock if Nvidia is pulling back support. The comments on the article were overwhelmingly negative, with many invoking dot-com vendor funding crashouts like Lucent and JDS-Uniphase. Admittedly, those comparisons did elicit some pushback, with the argument being that Nvidia has vastly more cash flow and vendor financing is not in and of itself suspect. Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web, a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites. The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience. It explores how storytelling, color, typography, imagery, and layout can work together to create websites that people recognize and remember. We asked Andy a few questions about the book and the ideas that went into it. I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them. Yet, somehow, so many websites look remarkably similar. I’m not suggesting every website needs a novelty design. Far from it. But I do think that — somewhere along the way—designers have become a little too comfortable with familiar patterns and predictable layouts. I wrote Standout Designs for the Web to encourage designers to rediscover the creativity and personality that made me fall in love with the web in the first place. Absolutely. Familiarity helps people understand how websites work, and there’s no reason to make something difficult to use just to be different. The problem is when familiarity makes every design look alike. When you visit a hotel website, an insurance company, or an online shop, you should be able to recognise something of the company behind it. I call this sameness “commodity design,” and it’s perfectly fine when all you want is fine, but it does little to make a company recognisable or its website memorable. I’m not arguing against using conventions. I’m asking designers to make more thoughtful decisions about when to use them. When I talk about storytelling, I don’t mean writing a lengthy company history or filling a website with marketing messages. Every company has a story worth telling. It might be how it started, the people behind it, its personality, or something unexpected about what it does. Those details can influence everything from the words you write to the colours, typography, illustrations, and layouts you choose. I spend a lot of time talking to clients because I’m looking for what makes them different. Sometimes, something they mention almost in passing becomes the inspiration for an entire design. The trick is recognising which details are worth developing and turning them into something visual. Ha! Because I wanted a vehicle for my explanations and to have some fun. Wheelman is a fictional company for getaway drivers, and it gave me the freedom to explore ideas without worrying too much about the practical constraints of a real client project. Its characters, criminal connections, and rather questionable business activities gave me plenty of opportunities to experiment with personality. But there’s a serious point behind the silliness. I use Wheelman to demonstrate how a company’s character can influence ordinary business pages, e-commerce, editorial content, and even transactional forms. If I can make a donation form for retired criminals interesting, designers have no reason not to bring more personality to everyday websites. I think twelve-column grids have become the default setting for web design. They’re familiar and useful, but they’re only one way to organise content. When designers begin every project with twelve columns, they’re already limiting their possibilities before they’ve considered what the content needs. In the book, I explore column, compound, and modular grids; ratios; symmetry versus asymmetry; and other ways to create rhythm and movement across a page. I’m not suggesting designers abandon column grids, but I want them to understand layout well enough to choose the right type and combine several—to make their layouts more interesting. I’d like them to approach their next project with a little more curiosity. Before opening Figma or Sketch, choosing a typeface, or deciding on a layout, I’d like them to spend more time discovering what makes the company they’re designing for interesting. Then I’d encourage them to question their first design decisions. Does this layout suit the content, or is it just familiar? Does this typography express the company’s personality? Can an illustration communicate something more effectively than an AI-generated image or a stock photo? I don’t expect every website to be extraordinary, and I certainly don’t think every design needs to break conventions. But I’d like designers to feel more confident making decisions that give their work character. You can purchase Standout Designs for the Web in the CSS-Tricks store.
