Credit: James Brittain/Getty In a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic is now claiming the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most important open problem in the field. The announcement came from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California company. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM). “If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford, UK, says. It would also be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800. The problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes.’ These are points on a plane denoted by z satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0. Riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he showed, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be. Alpöge’s 4-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, says that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November. “What he released is garbled,” Granville says of Alpöge’s document. Granville cites the downturn in the company’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.  “There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document. Over the last couple of decades, laptops have become the go-to computing device for those who want to break from a desktop but still need the right combination of software, connectivity, and performance. Entry-level models have become increasingly popular, as the needs of most laptop users are limited to typing, browsing the internet and social media, and keeping up to date with emails. Laptops are also capable of functioning as an entertainment device, though they can be somewhat cumbersome when used this way while out and about. Tablets can step in here. They've carved out a major piece of the mobile computing market, and offer more portability than a laptop. As well, many users find the touchscreen interface to be more intuitive than the mouse and cursor interaction that accompanies the use of a laptop. Tablets have become more and more powerful over the last decade, with high-end models capable of handling pro-level tasks like video editing. Tablets can be incredibly difficult to type on, however, and in most cases, tablet apps are scaled-down versions of laptop software. The best 2-in-1 laptops are meant to be the best of these two worlds. They come with a physical keyboard, trackpad, a touchscreen that folds back to give the device a more tablet-like form, and a number of different ways to hold it. 2-in-1 laptops offer a number of benefits over a standalone traditional laptop and a standalone tablet. But there's no perfect device out there, and 2-in-1 laptops have several disadvantages to consider, including pricing, durability, and limitations. The biggest draw of a 2-in-1 laptop is that it's essentially two devices bundled into one. From a pricing standpoint, that makes it a solid value play if you take advantage of both the laptop and touchscreen functionalities. But relative to its cousin devices, a 2-in-1 laptop is somewhat pricey. Entry-level 2-in-1s typically start in the $400 price range, though these are typically underspecced, with some models including just 4 GB of RAM and 64 GB of internal storage space. There are some entry-level laptops with 4 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage space that can be found in the $200 range, like the Lenovo Idea Tab. Mid-level 2-in-1s can be found in the $650 to $1,000 range, and some of these only double the RAM to 8 GB alongside various storage capacity increases. Additionally, upgrading specs comes with its own pricing scale, with premium 2-in-1-options like the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio 2 running upwards of $3,500. Configurations at this price will include much more impressive hardware like dedicated graphics cards, 32 GB of RAM, and 1 TB of storage space. However, high-end tablets and laptops are available for much less. The Apple iPad Pro 13-inch with an M5 processor and 2 TB of storage space is priced at $2,899, while laptops like the Dell Inspiron can be configured with an 8-core processor, 32 GB of RAM, and 1 TB of storage space for just $1,200. Because laptops and tablets are generally used on the go, build quality and durability matter in a different way than they do for desktop equipment. Alongside their standalone counterparts, 2-in-1 laptops are meant to be tossed into backpacks, sit on shifty legs for extended periods of time, and be opened and closed numerous times throughout the day. The basic open-and-close design of traditional laptops makes the wear and tear somewhat easy to handle, while tablets are designed and built with essentially no moving parts whatsoever. But with their 180-degree folding screen, and with the numerous positions in which they're meant to be held, 2-in-1 laptops often have more to survive. Unfortunately, not all 2-in-1 laptops come with the build quality users may be hoping for. The hinges are a more complicated design than the hinges of traditional laptops, and on entry-level 2-in-1 models — and even on some higher-end options — these parts are usually made of plastic. That can make these parts somewhat flimsy right out of the box, and with medium to heavy daily use, the hinges of cheaper 2-in-1 laptops are bound to lose sturdiness over time. 2-in-1 laptop models that feature a detachable display are susceptible to even more wear and tear, with the hinges and contact points wearing down every time the screen's detachable functionality is taken advantage of. Many 2-in-1 laptop users have made it their primary computing device because they're getting the benefits of a touchscreen interface alongside the software accessibility of a laptop computer. Since most 2-in-1s run on some version of Windows, they are entirely capable of running full laptop and PC software, including full versions of Microsoft Office, Adobe Creative Suite, and other commonly used software. Meanwhile, tablets often have scaled-down versions of such software, and they don't necessarily come with as much functionality. But for users excited to use this software in tandem with a 2-in-1 laptop's touchscreen, there may be a bit of a letdown. Having access to the software doesn't guarantee that it's designed to function any differently with a touchscreen. Most Windows programs are designed to be used with a mouse and cursor, and in most cases, using the software with a touchscreen simply means replacing the mouse with your finger. PCWorld has noted that only a handful of Windows apps are designed to truly take advantage of a touchscreen interface, and we've expressed that the lack of unoptimized apps is one good reason why there's simply no need for 2-in-1 laptops anymore. The tablet half of the 2-in-1 design may still be beneficial to some users, however, particularly those who aren't looking for user experience upgrades when it comes to the available software. Premium hardware is certainly available for 2-in-1 laptop users, and it's one of the perks of switching to a Microsoft Surface Laptop. But in a more general sense, the design of these computers can come with some compromises. Performance is often one of them. Not all 2-in-1 laptops are designed to be as slim as possible, but the ones that are can be short on space for the inclusion of complex cooling systems. Processors can't maintain peak performance in these 2-in-1 laptops, slowing down heavy workloads and CPU-intensive tasks. In the 2-in-1 space, manufacturers lean heavily on efficient processors that run cooler and consume less power. The design compromises for 2-in-1s can also result in smaller batteries being used. With the touchscreen already being more of a drain than the batteries of traditional laptops face, the battery life of a 2-in-1 laptop is a common disadvantage. Connection ports can also be in short supply. It's not uncommon to find entry-level and even mid-level options with only a few ports, and on truly budget models the only USB-C port available may be used for charging the device. This lack of connectivity may not be an issue for users who are more attuned to working with a tablet, but for those who plan to use a 2-in-1 as a total replacement for a workhorse laptop or a desktop PC, some sort of connection hub will likely need to accompany it. From a design standpoint, 2-in-1 laptops are meant to incorporate the best of two worlds. They have the touchscreen interface many users of the best big tablets love working with and, at the same time, provide a physical keyboard and trackpad, which are the kinds of features that users of laptops can find difficult to part ways with. Those who enjoy using 2-in-1 laptops will sometimes point specifically to the combining of the two form factors as a top attraction. Some of the best parts of a laptop are there when they're needed, while some of the best parts of a tablet are there for more on-the-go kinds of use. But one person's treasure is another's trash, and for some the 2-in-1 form factor may come across as clunky and awkward. When folded into tablet mode, the keyboard and trackpad end up on the back, and holding the device without inadvertently tapping keys or bumping the trackpad can be an annoyance. Using the touchscreen while in laptop mode can be similarly clumsy, with users needing to reach their arms out to interact with it, rather than simply having their hands and fingers already on the screen like they would in tablet mode. The form factor can also make a 2-in-1 laptop feel off balance or generally uncomfortable, as its center of gravity will change depending on which mode a user has it set up in.

As multiple technological routes toward artificial general superintelligence take shape, the regime beyond AGI is shifting from philosophical speculation to empirical research and governance questions. For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature. Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress. To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum. ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades). Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision. Yet knowing those upper limits doesnât tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, itâs hard to predict how capable a âgood enoughâ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human. What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both todayâs AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted. Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient. Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute, driven by three compounding factors: Multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world. At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year. A cognitive workload that can be performed by todayâs AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023. Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised. Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services. Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? Itâs certainly not a given, but practical ceilings on compute build-out, and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of todayâs AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now. Would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up todayâs AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own. Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI. Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways: Dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level. But some missing capabilities may be hard - or impossible - to patch over with sheer volume. While Einstein did figure out general relativity, a conference of one hundred thousand Ptolemaic astronomers probably wouldnât have. AI could follow four potential technological pathways to unlock previously unavailable cognitive capabilities. (For an in-depth discussion, see our From AGI to ASI report.) So far, qualitative capabilities have improved with remarkable consistency alongside model and data scale. This trend is captured by scaling laws that relate model performance to training compute, training data, and more recently, test-time compute (giving a model extra computing power to reason through a problem before answering). These scaling âlaws,â however, are extrapolations of observed trends that hold only within familiar boundaries, such as a particular model architecture, type of training data, and family of evaluations. They canât confidently predict the scale required for AGI or ASI, but we can identify potential bottlenecks to continued scaling of models and data: Todayâs dominant AI paradigm is to train large transformers to predict the next symbol in a long sequence across vast datasets, then refine them to learn to reason and follow instructions, and give them extra test-time compute. Recent research suggests this paradigm can, in principle, produce models that can run complex algorithms, including powerful learning algorithms, via their prompts - that is, without requiring retraining. This is a key ingredient for building AI systems at the theoretical upper limit of intelligence. But todayâs models fall short of humans on a few fundamental dimensions, including continual learning, certain forms of world modeling, decision-making, and sample efficiency - meaning that AI models need to be initially trained on much more data than humans to reach roughly the same intelligence level. They may also be missing the ability to invent genuinely new concepts and abstractions rather than recombining existing ones. Researchers are divided on whether these problems can be solved with simple extensions and evolutions of todayâs paradigm, or whether reaching ASI will require truly deep technological paradigm shifts. Human corporations, markets, and research communities solve problems that no individual could tackle alone. Similarly, coordinating thousands or millions of AGI instances into "group agents" or virtual agent economies could produce collective superintelligence. What is unclear today is how AI group intelligence could scale as we add more agents and compute, depending on how agents are organized. That is, we need multi-agent scaling laws. Early research finds clear intelligence gains in some tasks, but coordination inefficiencies still lead to diminishing returns as the population size grows. Less obviously, steering large agent collectives will require robust institutional design and organizational mechanisms, including defenses against accidental or intentional misinformation spread, manipulation, and collusion. Experiments with agent swarms are already demonstrating how quickly these dynamics can emerge, with individual agents learning to cheat and others acting as whistleblowers to expose them. Finally, AI systems could begin automating improvements to future generations of AI - a process known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) that was first discussed by I. J. Good and Ray Solomonoff. Unlike typical technological development, improvements to AI could directly speed up subsequent gains, leading to an accelerating rate of progress. However, further improvements in research tend to be âharder to findâ - more and more effort is required to maintain the same rate of improvement across technologies. Whether RSI leads to ârunawayâ progress is largely an empirical question. RSI is not a single process. It can operate via improvements to code and designs - from model architectures and training algorithms to chip layouts. It can also operate through data, by spending compute at deployment to produce improved results and outputs that can be reused to train future models. AlphaZero self-improved purely in this data driven way to reach superhuman performance. Finally, RSI can play out at the group level by dividing labor and specializing roles in an agent collective. A group of coordinated specialists can achieve more than the sum of what they could achieve as isolated generalists, in turn becoming more effective at finding further improvements. Instead of just scaling up a team with fixed roles, larger and more efficient collectives enable new types of specialization that were previously unviable - much like how a multi-cellular organism can support specialized organs like a heart or a brain, as opposed to a single-celled organism that perform all survival functions on its own. These three RSI mechanisms mirror evolutionary processes that drove the growth of human cognitive capabilities: genetic (code and design), cultural (data), and social evolution (group specialization through cooperation). Importantly, RSI loops can easily stall or degenerate if the feedback guiding them is poor. Pursuing ASI via recursive self-improvement therefore requires evaluation methods that can be rapidly scaled into the superhuman regime, where even large groups of humans can't easily assess AI outputs. Accordingly, RSI should advance fastest in domains that allow for automated verification without humans in the loop, such as mathematical proofs, while other domains might lag behind or taper off sooner. These pathways to ASI are not mutually exclusive - in fact, they compound on one another. If progress on one stalls, economic and geopolitical competition will likely shift effort toward the others. Even if RSI doesnât result in runaway gains, continued scaling in training data, speed, efficiency, and coordination could still drive rapid progress well beyond human-level AGI Because there are multiple routes to superintelligence, trying to slow down AI development by restricting just one area - like the computing power for training an AI model - won't be enough to stop overall progress. Equally, suppressing a single dimension risks creating a capability âoverhangâ: if multiple inputs need to be combined to make progress, holding back one dimension while the others move forward would lead to sudden, steep jumps in progress when the suppressed dimension is relaxed (or overcome otherwise). Taking all these arguments together, continued fast AI progress over the next decade is a serious possibility. It could take us relatively smoothly from today, to Expert AGI, and then into the superhuman AI regime, accelerating science and enabling breakthroughs in fields like medicine, materials, and clean energy. Even in the absence of dramatic frontier AI progress, cognitive industrialization alone could reshape knowledge work and the broader economy. Regardless of which path AI progress takes, we must anticipate far-reaching opportunities along with equally transformative pressures to many aspects of human society. None of these predictions are certain, but the pathways and scenarios are also far from unfounded hype or fiction. So what can be done? Our best course of action may sound familiar: model, measure, forecast, and repeat. While those steps arenât surprising, the complexity and scale of carrying them out on the road to ASI is entirely unprecedented. It requires large-scale and highly-interdisciplinary efforts across both frontier labs and national and global institutions. Many of the key metrics for tracking progress on these pathways require frontier-model access and sizable amounts of evaluation compute, alongside new benchmarking and modelling methodologies that could spawn entirely new research fields. Human-level AGI has long been the horizon for AI research, but it is far from the upper limit of intelligence. Understanding what could come next - and its implications across science, industry, and society - is the grand challenge ahead for researchers, developers, and policymakers. POPULAR SEARCHES                         BROWSE BY            When you help bring a franchise its first ever championship, unexpected opportunities tend to present themselves.  Earlier this month, for instance, Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold not only attended a Metallica concert at the Sphere in Las Vegas; he also got to meet the band. "And they knew what we did!" Arnold told me in amazement. "They’re like, ‘Wow, you guys are great!’ I’m like, ‘You guys are great!’" This is life now for Arnold after his Milwaukee Brewers won their first ever World Series title, despite the disadvantages presented by their 19th-ranked payroll.  Matt Arnold built the roster that led the Brewers to their first ever World Series. (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)  Ahead of an upcoming labor battle, the Brewers and Rays offered blueprints for success for teams incapable or unwilling to shop at the high end of the market under the current economic system.  "It was a good reminder of, ‘What wins baseball games?’" general manager J.J. Picollo, whose Royals ranked 18th in payroll last season, told me at the GM meetings earlier this month. "Good pitching. Good defense. Take advantage of opportunities when you have a chance to score. Situational hitting. Baserunning. These are all things that I think every team in baseball values, but when you’re in the market size that Milwaukee’s in or Tampa’s in or Kansas City’s in, it’s a good reminder that that’s the winning formula right there." Arnold and Milwaukee’s front office assembled a young, athletic group that frustrated opposing pitchers by selectively working long at-bats and finding ways on base. The Brewers forced mistakes by consistently putting the ball in play and causing havoc on the basepaths. They had the lowest chase rate in MLB, swung less overall than any team in the sport and ranked second in runs scored without relying on home runs — though they demonstrated fully capable of hitting those, too, when it counted in the postseason. As Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes pointed out: "We talk about them as this ‘small-ball’ team; they outhomered everybody in every series." Still, while the biggest spenders in the sport sought out sluggers who pulled the ball in the air, the Brewers bucked the trend during the regular season by emphasizing an approach in which they let the ball travel deep and shot it hard the other way, often on the ground. They hit the ball to the opposite field more than any team in MLB while still logging a higher hard-hit rate than the Braves, Phillies and Dodgers.  Will their success change the way teams develop their offensive philosophy? "There’s different ways to put together teams," said White Sox general manager Chris Getz, whose bottom-five payroll club made a surprise run to the postseason behind its power. "It really is leaning into the strengths of the group that you have." The Dodgers and their big payroll couldn't make it a World Series three-peat.(Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)  White Sox sluggers Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery hit more home runs than any player on the Brewers last year but also logged the highest strikeout rates in the sport. Getz will point out, however, that the presence of players such as Chase Meidroth, Sam Antonacci and Tristan Peters in the White Sox lineup help balance some of his team’s swing-and-miss.  "I think it’s important to have different types of hitters in a lineup," Getz said. "When you look at the postseason and the ALDS and the amount of strikeouts that we had, yeah, it was really hard to win a game that you really needed to win. You don’t want to reinvent the wheel. You don’t want to reinvent your team just because of a couple games or one series. Do we want to increase contact on our team? We absolutely do, and we’re putting things in place to improve contact. But we also don’t want it to come at the cost of scoring runs. You can score runs a lot of different ways." Of course, in Milwaukee’s case, some of the best pitching in the sport helped its cause, too.  The Brewers have become a model organization for development, unearthing gems in a multitude of ways. They signed outfielder Jackson Chourio as an international free agent in 2021 and have already watched the 22-year-old turn into the team’s all-time postseason leader in home runs and RBI. They drafted shortstop Cooper Pratt in the sixth round in 2023, gave him an eight-year extension in April of this year before he made his MLB debut, and watched him develop into a World Series standout.  Jacob Misiorowski won a World Series title and a Cy Young Award. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images)  They drafted Jacob Misiorowski out of Crowder College in the second round in 2022 and saw him ascend into the most unhittable starter in the sport and the National League Cy Young Award winner. They also drafted Aaron Ashby out of Crowder College in 2018 and saw him set a relief record with 18 scoreless innings in the 2026 postseason.  Ashby was a key piece in one of the greatest playoff bullpens ever constructed, a group that included another international free agent success story in Abner Uribe and one of many Brewers trade triumphs in closer Trevor Megill, who was acquired from the Twins for cash in 2023. The other top relief contributors in a Brewers bullpen that went 8-2 with a 1.38 ERA and eight saves in the postseason — JoJo Romero, DL Hall and Antonio Senzatela — also arrived via trade.  So, will small-market, lower-payroll teams try to replicate what the Brewers have built?  "I can only speak for the Royals," Picollo told me, "but the way they’ve constructed their roster is something we’ve been trying to do as well. We want to be as athletic as you can. We want to be good on the defensive side and baserunning, so there are goals that we have now." It’s easier said than done.  "The player pool, what’s available to you, may not allow you to have that," Picollo continued, referencing the presence of sluggers such as Vinnie Pasquantino and Salvador Perez on his Kansas City roster. "They’re bigger guys, not the guys that will steal 35 bases. We know that’s not going to be part of what they do. But even a guy like [Jac] Caglianone who’s a big, strong guy, he can run the bases well, and we’ve got to keep that expectation high that he needs to have that as something that’s in his toolbox so he can help us win games not just by hitting the ball out of the ballpark." Taylor Smith, the incoming president of baseball operations for an Athletics team that ranked in the bottom 10 in payroll last season, doesn’t think the Brewers’ and Rays’ success in 2026 will necessarily change how other small-market teams build their rosters.  "No, because we’ve seen these teams have a lot of success for a very long time," Smith told me. "I think we have already seen a lot of the copycat mentality of trying to take very talented people from both those organizations and try to bring some of that magic to running your own ballclub." One of Smith’s biggest moves after taking the A’s job was hiring Cam Castro, the Brewers’ senior vice president of player development and performance, to be his general manager. It’s one of many examples of teams hiring executives from successful smaller-market organizations to help run their franchises in recent years.   The Mets, for example, plucked David Stearns from the Brewers to be their president of baseball operations after the 2023 season. Meanwhile, former Rays executives are scattered throughout MLB, including the head of baseball operations for the Brewers (Arnold), Dodgers (Andrew Friedman), Cardinals (Chaim Bloom) and Marlins (Peter Bendix). Smith, too, started his professional career in the Rays’ front office.  "I think the two teams that we just saw in the World Series are teams that have really good information, they act on it very aggressively, and they do a great job of drafting, making trades, developing players," Smith told me at the GM meetings. "I think it’s a testament to the fact that you can still go out and have better information, make better decisions and win without some of the financial resources that some other teams have."  Do that well, and you never know what can happen.  You might even get to meet your favorite band.  "I know it sounds cliché, but it really is good people, the right mix of players and coaches and staff," Arnold told me when I asked him why this was the year for the Brewers' ascension. "There were just a lot of cool things that happened. We got hot at the right time and did something pretty special."  FOX SPORTS NEWSLETTER Follow your favorite leagues, teams and players for a personalized daily newsletter. Despite the fact that Moto Tag 2 has only been on the market for a few months at this point, Motorola is apparently getting Moto Tag 3 out in the not-too-distant future, and it’s already on sale (probably by mistake). An Amazon UK listing went up this week for “Moto Tag 3,” a new version of Motorola’s Android Find Hub tracker. The listing shows the tracker in “Pantone Lucent White,” while a second image shared by Evan Blass shows the new model in a vibrant purple color. There’s no indication of major changes in “Moto Tag 3,” with Motorola still claiming similar battery life, using a CR2032 battery, and supporting UWB in Android Find Hub. The listing (thanks Matt!) explains: Motorola moto tag 3 helps you locate everyday items with precision and reliability. Using Ultra Wideband and Bluetooth technology, it works with the Android Find Hub network to track belongings both nearby and at distance. With more than 500 days of battery life powered by a replaceable CR2032 battery, it is designed for long-term use. Built-in privacy protections, encrypted location data, and unwanted tracking alerts support secure tracking in a compact, IP68-rated design suitable for daily carry. “Moto Tag 3” is on sale from Amazon UK, though it comes with a “1-4 month” shipping estimate. This is almost certainly a slip-up, especially given the timing. This comes much earlier than expected. The original Moto Tag launched in 2024, with its sequel being announced in early 2026 before going on sale in the US less than six months ago in June 2026. Such an early move to “Moto Tag 3” is interesting, to say the least, so we’ll have to wait and see if there are any changes in tow beyond just the new colors. That said, these are really nice colors. It’s also possible this is just the same model with a slip-up in branding – the model number on the Amazon listing is unchanged. We’ll have to wait and see what happens. Moto Tag 2 did debut at CES in January, and with Razr Flex also in the works, Motorola almost certainly would launch an updated tracker at the trade show if it truly does plan to do so soon. This comes right as Moto Tag 2 has hit its lowest price ever at just $18.99 amid Black Friday sales.
